item.title: Renting a property well: strategies and tips for owners
item.description: Fast hosting doesn't mean good hosting. Learn how to protect your investment and choose reliable tenants.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The Ticino real estate market is moving. - Renting quickly does not mean renting well. - On June 1, 2025, 1% of Swiss homes were empty.
## Key facts - **What**: Renting a property well. - When: June 1, 2025. - Where: Switzerland, particularly Ticino. - Who: Property owners. - Amount: 1% of empty homes in Switzerland.
Renting quickly is easy. Renting well is another job. The Ticino market is moving, but more demand does not automatically mean fewer risks. Between a published ad and a well-rented property, there are price, presentation, speed, selection, and dossier control. Publishing four photos, writing “bright apartment,” and waiting for the phone to ring is not a real estate strategy. Sometimes it works. Sometimes it brings fifty messages in one evening, twenty requests without information, eight confirmed appointments, and three people who do not show up. Other times it brings a tenant quickly, but not the right one. And when the choice is wrong, the speed with which you rented immediately stops seeming like a success.
Because the real goal of an owner is not just to fill an apartment. It is to protect their income. To safeguard the value of the property. To choose a reliable person. To reduce downtime. To avoid mistakes that can accompany the lease relationship for years. This is the difference between renting and renting well.
### The market is running, but not running the same way everywhere
The last official census available, referring to June 1, 2025, records 48,455 empty homes in Switzerland, equal to 1% of the housing stock. The empty units offered for rent had decreased by 8% compared to the previous year. In Ticino, the rate of empty homes fell from 2.08% to 1.92%, the sharpest contraction among the Swiss major regions. The Ticino market is not a single block. It's a multi-speed market. An analysis published in March 2026 describes sustained demand in the most attractive areas, particularly in Lugano, but highlights strong differences between regions, municipalities, neighbourhoods and types of properties. An attic in the centre of Lugano does not position itself as a large suburban apartment. A furnished two-room apartment does not speak to the same audience as a family home. A valuable item can't be presented as just any listing. And a correct price on a street can be wrong just two neighborhoods away.
The market is moving, yes. But it moves especially for those who know how to read it. The difference between renting and renting well lies in the ability to understand the dynamics of the market and adapt to its needs. This means not only publishing a listing, but also presenting the property in the right way, selecting potential tenants carefully and carefully checking their dossier.
### Practical Implications for Owners
For property owners, renting well means protecting their investment. This means choosing reliable tenants who regularly pay their rent and respect the property. In addition, it is important to reduce downtime between tenants to maximize income. Hosting well takes time and attention, but the long-term benefits are significant.

item.title: Starting a business in Graubünden: costs and procedures
item.description: Complete guide: legal forms, registration in the trade register, federal and cantonal taxes, VAT, AVS obligations, SUVA, LAMal. Step-by-step procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Three main legal forms: sole proprietorship, simple partnership, limited liability company (LLC) - Mandatory registration with the Canton of Graubünden commercial register - Variable costs depending on canton and legal form; taxation at three levels - Insurance obligations: AHV (9.8%), LAMal, SUVA if you have employees
## Key facts - **What**: Opening a business in the Canton of Graubünden - Where: Canton commercial register + federal and cantonal tax authorities - Who: Sole proprietorship, simple partnership or LLC - Capital: No minimum for sole proprietorship; variable for partnerships - Obligations: AHV registration, LAMal, SUVA (if employees), annual tax returns
### The legal forms: the fundamental choice
Opening a business in the Canton of Graubünden first requires choosing the legal form. In Switzerland, the main forms are four: sole proprietorship, simple partnership, limited liability company (LLC) and public limited company (PLC).
The sole proprietorship is managed by a single person, who is personally and unlimitedly liable for the company's debts. It does not require a minimum capital and is the simplest structure to set up, but offers less asset protection: the owner's personal credit is exposed to business risks.
The simple partnership (SP) involves at least two partners and is suitable for small collaborations. It does not require a formal minimum capital and provides unlimited and joint liability of the partners, meaning each partner is personally liable for the company's debts.
The limited liability company (LLC) is the most common form for small and medium-sized enterprises. It offers protection of the personal liability of the partners up to the capital contributed. It requires a notarial deed of incorporation and mandatory registration with the commercial register. It is suitable for those who wish to separate personal and business assets.
The public limited company (PLC) is more complex, suitable for companies with high capital. It requires a corporate governance structure (board of directors, shareholders' meeting) and higher capitalization.
### Registration with the Canton commercial register
In the Canton of Graubünden, as in the rest of Switzerland, registration with the commercial register is mandatory for all forms of partnerships and for sole proprietorships that carry out commercial activities (excluding non-commercial liberal professions). Registration produces a publicity effect and, for partnerships, confers legal personality.
The required documents depend on the form. For a sole proprietorship, personal data, a description of the activity and a copy of the identity card are needed. For an LLC, the notarial deed of incorporation, the minutes of the constituent assembly and the data of the partners and managers are required.
The registration fees are set at the cantonal level and vary significantly between the twenty-six Swiss cantons. The procedure with the Canton commercial register office usually takes 1–2 weeks. ### Taxation at three levels: federal, cantonal, municipal
Anyone exercising a commercial activity in Switzerland is subject to three levels of taxes: federal direct tax (FDT), cantonal tax, and municipal tax. In the canton of Graubünden, the cantonal rate is determined by the canton itself, while each municipality applies its own multiplier to the cantonal taxable income. This system means that two entrepreneurs in the same canton but in different municipalities can have slightly different tax burdens.
The FTA (Federal Tax Administration) collects the FDT, while the cantonal administration of Graubünden manages the cantonal tax and reports to the relevant municipalities. Each entrepreneur must submit an annual declaration to the federal tax authorities (by the cantonal deadline, usually late February/early March) and provide complete accounting.
### Insurance and contribution obligations
**Professional pension AVS/AI** is mandatory for self-employed workers. The rate is 9.8% on the net income of the activity (income minus costs). It is not withheld from salary (unlike employees, who pay 5.3% of AVS/AI) and is paid directly to the cantonal AVS fund. Registration is free and must be done within three months of starting the activity.
Professional pension LPP is not mandatory for self-employed workers without employees. However, if you hire employees, you are required to offer professional pension in accordance with federal law. The rate is divided by age groups: 7% for 25–34 years, 10% for 35–44, 15% for 45–54, and 18% for 55 years until the reference age (65 for men, 64 for women).
Accident insurance (SUVA/LAA) is mandatory only if the company has employees and exercises non-agricultural activities. The rate varies between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector and specific risk. For the self-employed worker without employees, coverage is optional but strongly recommended.
Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for all residents in Switzerland, including entrepreneurs. Unlike AVS and LPP, it is not a salary contribution but a private insurance with a per capita premium. In the canton of Graubünden, premiums vary by geographic region and by chosen deductible (CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 or 2500 annually). The canton provides subsidies to those with low total income.
### Registration with the competent authorities
Registration with AVS as a self-employed worker is done with the cantonal AVS fund of Graubünden or with a private compensation fund recognized by the UFAS/BSV. SUVA is the single insurance entity for accidents in Switzerland. If you hire employees, they must be registered with AVS within three months of the start of the employment relationship.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Opening procedure in 7 steps
Step 1: Choosing the legal form Evaluate whether to operate as a sole proprietorship (unlimited liability, less bureaucracy) or as a company (asset protection, greater administrative complexity). For a company (Ltd, SA), a notarial deed will be required.
Step 2: Verifying cantonal requirements Consult the cantonal administration of Graubünden to verify if the activity sector requires special permits or authorizations (business license, health authorization, license for certain sectors, etc.).
Step 3: Registration with the Commercial Register Submit the documents to the cantonal Commercial Register office of Graubünden. Prepare: copy of a valid ID, detailed description of the activity, and (for companies) the notarial deed. The procedure usually takes 1–2 weeks. Once registered, you will receive a registration certificate.
Step 4: Registration with AVS Contact the cantonal AVS fund of Graubünden or a recognized private compensation fund. Provide your personal data, a description of the activity, and the estimated income for the first year. Registration is free and generates an AVS insurance number (retirement number).
Step 5: Insurance coverage If you hire employees, registration with SUVA occurs automatically; you will pay the monthly premiums. Take out private health insurance within 3 months of residence in Switzerland (if you are new to the country). Also consider professional liability insurance to protect your personal assets.
Step 6: Registration with tax authorities Once registered with the Commercial Register, the federal (AFC/ESTV) and cantonal tax authorities are automatically notified. You will receive forms for the annual income declaration. If you hire employees, request a compensation number to pay the AVS/AI contributions of the employees.
Step 7: Registration as an employer (if hiring) If you intend to hire your first employee, register with the cantonal register office. Each employee must be registered with AVS within three months of the start of the employment relationship. You will need to provide a monthly salary certificate and pay the AVS/AI contributions.
### Critical deadlines and recurring obligations
LAMal registration: mandatory within 3 months of arrival in Switzerland. Failure to meet this deadline results in significant fines.
Annual tax declaration: must be submitted by the deadlines set by the canton of Graubünden (usually by February 28 or March 31 of the following year). Keep all accounting documentation for at least 7 years.
VAT payment: if the annual turnover exceeds CHF 100,000, VAT registration becomes mandatory. You will need to pay VAT on a monthly or quarterly basis according to the system registered with the AFC/ESTV. Purchase and service costs become deductible (VAT credit).
AVS contribution payment: pay monthly or quarterly to the cantonal AVS fund, according to the schedule set by the compensation fund.
For specialized support, contact the cantonal Commercial Register of Graubünden or an external tax consultant (fees are deductible from taxable income). Many municipal administrations offer free guidance services to new entrepreneurs.
Use the [tax and contribution calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the tax and contribution burden according to the estimated income of your activity.

item.title: Buying a Valais house: prices, mortgage and costs
item.description: Guide to buying property in Valais: own funds required, mortgage sustainability, transfer taxes and notary fees.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Buying a house in Switzerland requires at least 20% of personal funds - Mortgages must comply with federal sustainability criteria - Each canton applies different taxes on transfers and properties - Notary fees and costs vary by canton
## Key facts - **What**: Real estate purchase - When: Process 3-6 months from search to deed - Where: Swiss cantons (including Valais) - Who: Buyer, banks, notary, land registry - Amount of personal funds: Minimum 20% of purchase price
### The four pillars of real estate purchase Buying a house in Switzerland means navigating four crucial areas: availability of personal funds, mortgage capacity, differentiated taxation, and additional costs. Each of these areas is regulated differently at the federal, cantonal, and municipal levels — no data is the same from one canton to another.
The Swiss tax system operates on three levels: federal direct tax, cantonal tax, and municipal taxes. Each canton, including Valais, has its own tax laws and multipliers. Taxes are not centralized: each canton decides its own criteria, especially regarding property transfer taxes. Similarly, credit institutions apply mortgage sustainability criteria that are inspired by federal principles but vary in maximum amounts and conditions. Notary fees, finally, do not follow a fixed national tariff: they depend on the amount of the transaction and the tariffs set by the competent canton.
### Why prices vary between cantons Valais, like every Swiss canton, has its own real estate market with specific dynamics. Local factors such as housing demand, availability of buildable land, economic attractiveness, and proximity to urban centers influence average prices. Comparing the price per square meter in Valais with that of Zurich or Geneva makes no sense: the market is deeply local. Consulting the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) to compare different areas helps you understand regional differences better.
When looking for "average prices" in a canton, you should always check current data with local real estate agencies, listing sites, or regional economic research institutes. Prices change over time and vary enormously even within zones of the same canton. ### Fondamenti del mutuo ipotecario in Svizzera
Il mutuo ipotecario svizzero si basa su due concetti centrali: il rapporto LTV (loan-to-value) e la sostenibilità del debito.
**Il rapporto LTV** è la percentuale del valore immobiliare che una banca è disposta a prestare. Una regola federale ampiamente adottata è che i fondi propri devono essere almeno il 20% del prezzo di acquisto. Questo significa che se compri una casa per CHF 500.000, devi avere almeno CHF 100.000 di risorse proprie. Il restante CHF 400.000 può provenire dal mutuo. Alcune banche richiedono fondi propri ancora maggiori — fino al 25-30% o oltre — specialmente in mercati con elevato rischio di calo dei prezzi. Altre applicano condizioni diverse a seconda della situazione economica personale dell'acquirente.
La sostenibilità del debito è il secondo pilastro. Una banca non ti presta una somma arbitraria: valuta se il tuo reddito è sufficiente a ripagare il mutuo. Il criterio tipico è che la rata mensile del mutuo non deve superare una certa percentuale del reddito lordo (spesso il 33-35%, ma varia). Oltre alla rata del mutuo, la banca considera anche tasse sulla proprietà (variabili per cantone e comune), premi assicurativi sulla casa, costi di manutenzione ordinaria e costi di riscaldamento e utenze. Se la somma di tutti questi importi supera il limite di sostenibilità, la banca dice no, anche se tecnicamente avresti il 20% di fondi propri.
### Calcolare la sostenibilità del mutuo
Supponiamo un acquirente con un reddito annuo lordo di CHF 80.000. Se la banca applica il criterio del 33%, la rata massima del mutuo dovrebbe essere circa CHF 2.200 al mese. Usa il [calcolatore di mutuo](nav:calculator) per stimare le rate mensili in base al tuo reddito e al tasso di interesse corrente. Se l'acquirente deve pagare anche CHF 300 di tasse annuali e CHF 200 di assicurazione e manutenzione, il margine si riduce ulteriormente. Questa semplificazione mostra perché due acquirenti con lo stesso apporto di fondi propri possono ottenere mutui di importi diversi: dipende dal reddito, dalle tasse regionali, dai tassi di interesse correnti, e dai criteri specifici della banca.
Tutte le banche svizzere si confrontano anche con gli orientamenti della BNS (Banca nazionale svizzera) sulla politica dei tassi e sui rischi macroeconomici. Questi orientamenti non stabiliscono un tetto massimo di finanziamento, ma influenzano le condizioni generali di mercato.
### Costi aggiuntivi e imposte
Oltre al prezzo della casa e al mutuo, bisogna contare: 1) Imposta sui trapassi di proprietà: Varia fortemente tra cantoni. Alcuni cantoni applicano un'imposta sull'atto di acquisto (variabile dal 0,5% al 2% del prezzo), altri non l'applicano affatto. Il Vallese, come ogni cantone, ha una propria legislazione; 2) Spese notarili: Necessarie per il rogito (atto notarile che trasferisce la proprietà). Le tariffe sono stabilite dalla legislazione cantonale e dipendono dal valore immobiliare; 3) Valutazione immobiliare: La banca richiede una perizia per verificare il valore della casa. Costo: variabile, solitamente da CHF 800 a CHF 2.000; 4) Assicurazione della casa: Obbligatoria durante il mutuo. Il premio è proporzionale al valore immobiliare e alla zona geografica; 5) Iscrizione al registro fondiario: Costo amministrativo per registrare la proprietà al catasto cantonale. Tutti questi costi variano per cantone e non possono essere calcolati senza riferimenti specifici locali.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### The step-by-step procedure
**Step 1: Financial capacity check** — Before starting to look for a house, meet with a bank and ask for a "pre-approval" of the mortgage. You will state your income, your savings, your credit history, and the bank will tell you the maximum amount it can lend you. This document (pre-approval letter) is useful when making an offer: the seller knows you are a serious buyer.
Step 2: Property search — Use real estate portals, local agencies, notary ads (who often manage inheritances). Check that the price is in line with the local market by consulting historical sales data.
Step 3: Offer and preliminary sales contract — When you find the house, make a written offer. If the seller accepts, sign a "preliminary contract" (the name varies by canton: "promise of sale", "compromise", etc.). This contract binds both parties and sets the price, the date of the deed, and the conditions (e.g., "subject to obtaining the mortgage").
Step 4: Official mortgage application — Provide the bank with all documents: last 2-3 years of tax returns, last 3 months of pay slips, bank statements, list of current debts. The bank assesses the risk and communicates the approved amount, interest rate, and mortgage duration (usually 15-25 years).
Step 5: Property valuation — The bank appoints an expert to value the house to verify its actual value. If the valuation is lower than the agreed price, the bank may reduce the mortgage offered, and you would have to cover the difference with more of your own funds or renegotiate the price.
Step 6: Signing of the notarial deed — The notary prepares the official deed of transfer of ownership. You, the seller, the notary, and the bank representative meet to sign. The notary transmits the signatures to the cantonal land registry, which registers the new owner. At this point, the property is officially yours.
Step 7: Registration and completion — The bank disburses the mortgage (the amount is transferred to the seller's account). You pay the transfer taxes and notary fees. The bank registers a "mortgage" on the property (the right to seize it if you do not pay the installments).
### Essential documents
When looking for a mortgage, be prepared to provide a passport or ID, last 3-5 years of tax returns, last 3 months of pay slips (if employed), latest tax return (if self-employed), bank statements for the last 3 months, list of debts (credit cards, car loans, etc.), and a work certificate attesting to your employment and salary. Some banks also require a statement of assets (lists of investments, owned houses, insurance policies).
### Role of the notary and overall times
The notary is not an "optional middleman": it is mandatory by federal law (Code of Obligations, article 257). It verifies the ownership of the house, checks that there are no previous mortgages engaged, ensures that the deed complies with cantonal legislation, deposits the deed with the land registry office, and communicates the transfer to the canton (for transfer taxes). From when you sign the preliminary contract to when you receive the keys usually takes 2-4 months. The notary needs time to verify the ownership of the property, check that there are no previous mortgage debts, and prepare the documentation. The bank needs time for the valuation and final approval.
### Tools to deepen
Once you have identified the canton, check the website of the cantonal land registry office for registration fees, the website of the cantonal notary chamber for notary fees, and the website of the cantonal finance administration for transfer taxes and cantonal property tax. If you are planning a purchase, use the [mortgage calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the monthly installments based on different rates and durations.

item.title: Canton Valais Scholarships: how to get them
item.description: Guide to scholarships in the canton of Valais: general requirements, where to look for information and how to apply to the cantonal authorities.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The Valais provides scholarships and study loans with annual deadlines - Requirements and maximum amounts change every year - The competent cantonal office is the main point of contact
## Key facts - **What**: Scholarships and study loans in the canton of Valais - Who pays: Cantonal Authority of Valais - When: Deadlines defined annually - Where: Competent cantonal office - Requirements: Economic situation, residence, academic merit (generally)
The canton of Valais, like every Swiss canton, has its own system of scholarships and study loans. Financial resources for student support are managed at the cantonal level, which means that the requirements, maximum amounts payable and deadlines for submitting applications vary from other cantons and are updated annually.
### The Swiss cantonal system of study support
Scholarships in Switzerland do not follow a uniform federal standard. Each canton independently defines the access criteria, the maximum amounts, the duration of the subsidy and the methods of submitting applications. The Valais, as part of this federalist system, has exclusive competence over its policy of support for young people in training.
This means that a student who resides in Valais and attends a recognized educational institution can apply directly to the competent cantonal office. ### General requirements that influence access
The Swiss cantons, in defining their criteria for access to scholarships, generally consider some common factors. The economic factor is the main criterion: the family's financial situation determines eligibility. Each canton sets an income or wealth threshold below which it is assumed that the student is entitled to a grant. Valais, like other cantons, applies specific economic capacity tests. If you want to understand how your tax situation affects potential eligibility, consult [the tax return guide](nav:tax-return). Since these values change annually (often in relation to inflation and the cost of living), it is essential to consult the cantonal office directly to know the current thresholds.
The academic factor is considered by almost all cantons: students must have sufficient school results. It is not necessary to obtain excellent grades, but it is important to demonstrate a serious commitment and consistent progress in the course of study.
The residence factor represents another crucial aspect. Normally, the student must reside in the canton and be a Swiss citizen or, if foreign, have specific residence requirements depending on international agreements and cantonal regulations.
Finally, the study level factor: Valais supports students in different educational cycles, from those in vocational training to university students. However, the amounts and methods may differ depending on the type of training followed.
### How they vary from canton to canton
A crucial element to understand is that the scholarship system is built in a federal way: each canton has full autonomy. This entails significant variations between Valais and other cantons (Zurich, Bern, Geneva, Vaud, Basel) in terms of maximum amounts disbursable per year, number of years of support, combination between scholarships and loans, criteria for evaluating school merit, and disbursement timelines.
A Valais student who moves to another canton for study reasons may find themselves having to reconsider their application based on the rules of the new location. Similarly, a student coming from another canton who moves to Valais will have access to Valais scholarships only after meeting the local residence requirements.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Step-by-step procedure to find specific information
Since the specific details (exact amounts, precise deadlines, complete list of required documents) change every year and are only available from the cantonal authorities, here is how to proceed.
The first step is to identify the exact name and contact of the Valais office responsible for scholarships. This office may vary in name and organizational structure, but it generally depends on the Department of Education or a similar authority. Searching on the official website of the canton of Valais will provide the email address and phone number.
Once the office is identified, request the official documents for the current academic year. These documents will include the official application form, a detailed description of the current requirements, maximum amounts per student category, submission deadlines, and a complete list of documents to be attached (income certificates, bank statements, report cards, etc.).
The required documents generally include tax certificates, documentation on the family's economic situation, and documents proving enrollment in a recognized educational institution. Valais may also require a declaration of the family's income and assets. Deadlines are annual and communicated by the cantonal authorities: it is essential to respect the communicated terms, as late applications may not be considered.
After submission, the cantonal office will review the application and communicate the decision. This process can take several weeks.
### Part-time work during studies
Many students supplement the support from scholarships with part-time work. If you are interested in this option, consult [job listings in Switzerland](nav:jobs) to find positions compatible with study schedules.
### Commonly requested documents
Although the exact list depends on Valais' annual rules, the documents commonly requested in Swiss cantons include a residence certificate, a criminal record extract (in some cases), income and asset certificates of the family (last 2 years), proof of enrollment in an educational institution, report cards or academic merit certificates, a copy of an identity document, and income declaration (if available).
A practical tip: many Swiss cantons, including Valais, provide standardized forms for requesting certificates from cantonal tax and statistical offices. Contact the scholarship office directly to avoid delays due to incomplete documentation.
If you wish to verify your cost of living situation and how this affects your potential eligibility, you can consult [cost of living data in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) to get a clearer picture of the national economic situation. Additionally, the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) can help you understand your economic context.
Contacting the Valais office directly is the most effective way to obtain precise, up-to-date information tailored to your specific situation.

item.title: Rentals in Graubünden: average fees and rental law
item.description: Complete guide to the right to rent in Graubünden: fees, security deposit, cancellation and dispute according to Swiss federal rules.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Maximum security deposit of 3 months' rent in a blocked account - Contest the rent within 30 days to the conciliation authority - Notice of termination only valid on the official cantonal form
## Key facts - **What**: Federal tenancy law (Code of Obligations, art. 253 and following) - Where: Applicable in all cantons, including Graubünden - Who: Tenants and landlords, protected by federal law - Security deposit: Maximum 3 months' rent - Contestation deadline: 30 days to the conciliation authority - Termination: Only on the official cantonal form, nothing else
### Federal tenancy law in Switzerland
In Switzerland, tenancy law is regulated at the federal level by the Code of Obligations (CO), articles 253 and following. This means that the same rules apply in all cantons, including the canton of Graubünden, ensuring uniform protection for tenants and landlords. There are no substantial differences from canton to canton regarding fundamental rights: what is prohibited for a landlord in Graubünden is also prohibited in Zurich or Geneva. Federal law prevails over any cantonal exception and represents the normative framework on which eventual regional integrations are based.
The security deposit is one of the central pillars of this legal protection. A maximum of 3 months' rent can be withheld as a guarantee against damage or non-payment by the tenant. This figure is not just a market recommendation but an absolute legal limit: no landlord can ask for more. The deposit must be paid into a blocked account in the tenant's name, not the landlord's, not mixed. This mechanism concretely protects the tenant: the money remains formally the tenant's property, although the landlord can access it for documented and proven damages or payment arrears.
The termination of the contract by the lessor (landlord) is valid exclusively if communicated through the official cantonal form. Each canton, including Graubünden, provides the form compliant with federal law and cantonal regulations. This document is provided by the competent cantonal administration. A termination written on plain paper, even if dated and signed, is not legally valid and does not produce a legal effect.
If the tenant considers the initial rent manifestly excessive, they have the right to contest it within 30 days of receiving the information. The contestation must be submitted to the conciliation authority for tenancy matters in their canton. This procedure is fundamental to verify the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) and assess whether the rent is sustainable compared to their income and the local market standard. ## The security deposit: protection and return
The security deposit is a central instrument in the lease agreement. Paid at the beginning of the lease, it must remain in a restricted account in the tenant's name for the entire duration of the contract. During the lease, the owner cannot access these funds for ordinary or extraordinary expenses of the property: the account is blocked until the end of the contractual relationship. Only in the event of proven damage to the dwelling or accumulated rent debts, the owner can request partial restitution through a formal procedure, communicating the reasons to the tenant.
Once the contract is concluded and the tenant has vacated the dwelling, the landlord has 30 days to return the deposit in full. If there is damage deemed to be the responsibility of the tenant, the landlord may withhold a portion equivalent to the cost of the repair, but must clearly document what the damage is and communicate to the tenant the reasons for the withholding in writing. If the landlord returns less than the due amount without justification or delayed more than 30 days, the tenant may appeal to the conciliation authority within the established deadlines.
### Dispute the initial fee
Not all rentals are the same, even in similar geographic areas. The Code of Obligations allows the tenant to challenge a fee that he considers manifestly excessive. “Manifestly excessive”

If you need to address a dispute regarding rent, deposit, or lease conditions, follow these concrete steps.
Step 1: Verify the regulatory situation Read your lease agreement carefully and identify the specific point of the dispute. Is the initial rent considered excessive compared to the local market? Has the landlord returned the deposit incompletely without documented justification? Has the landlord sent a termination notice on plain paper, not on the official cantonal form? Each case requires a different approach and a different legal basis.
Step 2: Communicate with the landlord in writing Before turning to the conciliation authority, write a formal letter (preferably registered mail with return receipt) to the landlord, clearly and documentedly outlining your complaint. For example: "I contest the monthly rent as it is manifestly excessive compared to comparable dwellings in the area. I enclose a price comparison of similar properties in the same area." This communication creates a documented trail and often resolves the dispute directly.
**Step 3: Gather documents** - Copy of the original lease agreement - Written communication from the landlord regarding the rent or dispute - Receipts for the security deposit payments - Photographs of any disputed damages (if relevant) - Copy of the written communication to the landlord (Step 2) - Price comparison of similar dwellings in the same area (if contesting the initial rent) - Witness statements (if applicable)
Step 4: Turn to the conciliation authority In Graubünden, the conciliation authority for lease matters is with the cantonal administration. You can contact them through the official cantonal website or by phone. You will submit your complaint within the legal deadlines (30 days for contesting the initial rent). The conciliation authority will guide you through the local procedure, response times, and any potential costs of the procedure.
Step 5: Consider legal recourse (if necessary) If the conciliation authority does not resolve the dispute in your favor, or if the dispute involves significant amounts, you can appeal to the cantonal civil courts. This step requires specialized legal advice and involves procedural costs. Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to verify if the dispute justifies the legal costs and time invested.
### Termination and legal deadlines
The landlord's termination of the contract must be communicated in writing, on the official cantonal form, with the following notice periods: - 1 month during the first year of the lease - 2 months from the second to the ninth year of the lease - 3 months from the tenth year of the lease onwards
The termination must also respect the termination periods established by cantonal law: in many cantons (including Graubünden), termination is only possible at the end of the month or on specific dates. Failure to comply with these terms renders the termination null and void. Verify the exact local rules with the cantonal administration.
### Where to find help and resources
The conciliation authority for lease matters is the first point of contact for disputes regarding rent and leases. If you cannot find it online, contact the Graubünden cantonal administration or the municipal office where you reside directly. For complex legal interpretation issues or high-value disputes, consult a lawyer specialized in lease law.

item.description: Purchase in Graubünden: own funds 20-30%, mortgage loan up to 80%, variable transport tax per municipality, notary fees 1-2%. Explained procedure and costs.

## In brief - Own funds: at least 20% of the purchase price - Mortgage: up to 80%, duration 15-25 years, variable rates - Transfer tax: varies by canton and Grisons municipality
## Key facts - **What**: Purchase of real estate in Grisons - Where: Canton of Grisons, Eastern Switzerland - Who: Swiss residents or foreigners authorized by SEM - Own funds: 20-30% of the price (savings, LPP, pillar 3a) - Additional costs: Transfer tax + notary + land registry (1-3% total)
In the canton of Grisons, anyone wishing to buy a house must have own funds equal to at least 20 percent of the purchase price. The rest is financed through a mortgage from a bank. At the time of acquisition, the transfer tax (cantonal and municipal), notary fees, and land registry taxes are added. These three elements represent the core of the financial planning for those intending to buy in Grisons.
Own funds can come from three sources: personal savings, withdrawal from the second pillar (LPP/BVG) for the purchase of the main residence, and withdrawal from the third pillar 3a. The withdrawal from LPP is subject to time constraints: it must occur at most 5 years before ordinary retirement. The third pillar 3a is available at any time to finance a main property. These withdrawals do not increase the federal taxable income (IFD) in the same year but may have tax implications at the cantonal and municipal level according to the laws of Grisons.
### Mortgage structure
The mortgage is governed by the Code of Obligations at the federal level, ensuring uniformity among Swiss cantons. The bank provides the financing against the registration of a lien in the land register. The registration of the mortgage protects the bank and allows the borrower to acquire the property once the price is paid in cash or through financing. The mortgage is usually granted at variable or fixed rates for periods of 3, 5, or 10 years. Once the debt is paid off, the bank cancels the mortgage from the register.
To the purchase price are added three categories of unavoidable costs:
1. Transfer tax: A cantonal and municipal tax on the transfer of real estate. In the canton of Grisons, as in all Swiss cantons, the rate varies by municipality. The final amount depends on the purchase price and the specific rate of the Grisons municipality where the property is located.
2. Notary fees: Necessary to authenticate the sales contract and register the property in the land register. They are regulated at the cantonal level and generally amount to 1-2 percent of the purchase price.
3. Land registry and administrative taxes: Include registration in the land registry and other municipal procedures for the acquisition of the property.
Those buying in Grisons must contact the cantonal and municipal tax administration to know the exact transfer tax rate applicable to the specific municipality where the property is located. ### Mortgage sustainability and banking criteria
Swiss banks apply strict sustainability criteria before making a loan. The general rule is that the monthly installment (principal plus interest) should not exceed 33 percent of the buyer's gross income. Income is calculated net of direct federal taxes (DFI), cantonal and municipal taxes specific to Graubünden. Those with a low income after tax deductions will find it difficult to access a large mortgage.
To calculate your tax burden in Graubünden, you need to consider three levels of taxation. The direct federal tax (DFI) is calculated on the basis of total income and is uniform in Switzerland according to the rates set by the Federal Council. The cantonal income tax of Graubünden varies according to the canton and its specific laws. Finally, the municipal tax uses a multiplier that amplifies the cantonal taxable amount: each municipality in Graubünden has its own multiplier that determines the effective municipal rate.
An example of calculation: if the annual gross income is CHF 80'000 and the total tax burden (federal + cantonal + municipal) is 20 percent, the net income is CHF 64'000. The maximum sustainable monthly installment is CHF 64,000 × 0.33 ÷ 12 = approximately CHF1,760. For an installment of CHF 1,760, the sustainable mortgage is aboutCHF 350,000-400,000 depending on the current interest rates in the Swiss mortgage market.

The real estate purchase procedure in Graubünden follows a fixed order regulated by federal law and cantonal regulations. The first step is to search for the property on the real estate market. The main portals (ImmoScout24, Homegate, NxImmo) list available properties in Graubünden with prices, technical characteristics (square footage, year of construction, number of rooms), and photos.
Once the property is identified, a purchase proposal is signed, sometimes called a non-binding offer. This proposal specifies the proposed price and preliminary terms (transfer date, suspensive conditions such as mortgage financing). If the seller accepts, the proposal becomes binding, and the subsequent steps must be completed within the agreed terms.
The second crucial step is the pre-approval of the mortgage with a bank. Before signing the final contract, contact a bank to obtain a pre-approval letter for financing. The bank requires income documentation (last 2-3 years of tax returns, current pay slips), a list of current debts, bank statements (assets), and a preliminary appraisal report of the property. This step is crucial as it quickly identifies sustainability obstacles.
### Signing the contract and land registry
The third step is signing the final sales contract. The contract is drafted by a notary's office or the seller's real estate administration. It includes the final price, the property transfer date (usually 30-60 days after signing), special conditions such as the extinction of existing mortgages, easements, third-party rights, and maintenance responsibilities until the transfer date. Both parties (seller and buyer) sign the contract before a notary, who authenticates the signature and keeps a copy in their archive.
The fourth step is the mortgage disbursement by the bank. Once all contractual conditions and documentation are verified, the bank disburses the mortgage to the buyer via bank transfer. The amount is deposited into a notary's deposit account, a blocked account in the notary's name, which holds it until the property transfer.
The fifth step is the payment of the price and the property transfer. The buyer pays the price to the seller through the notary's deposit account. The notary verifies the payment and proceeds with the property registration in the land registry in the buyer's name. The registration is an administrative act regulated at the federal level that certifies the property transfer and is mandatory under Swiss law.
The sixth step is the payment of taxes and ancillary expenses. The buyer pays the transfer tax to the cantonal or communal administration of Graubünden according to the applicable rate for the specific municipality. Notary fees are paid directly to the notary's office. The bank also requires the activation of mandatory property insurance to protect the building from fire and damage, a necessary condition for mortgage release.
### Where to find information and support
To know the average prices in Graubünden, consult national real estate portals (ImmoScout, Homegate) or the Graubünden Cantonal Bank, which publishes regional real estate statistics. The Ticino Statistical Office (USTAT) provides data on neighboring cantons, useful for market trend comparisons.
For cantonal tax legislation in Graubünden, contact the cantonal tax office, which specifies transfer tax rates for each municipality, tax deductions, and income declaration procedures. For current mortgage rates, consult major Swiss banks: UBS, Raiffeisen, Graubünden Cantonal Bank, Cantonal Savings Bank. Rates vary daily based on international market conditions and decisions by the SNB (Swiss National Bank).
You can estimate the sustainability of your financial situation using the [mortgage calculator](nav:calculator), a tool that integrates your income, current debts, and the expected purchase amount to determine the sustainable monthly installment and the maximum accessible mortgage.

item.title: Buying a house in Graubünden: prices, equity and mortgages
item.description: Guide to buying real estate in the Canton of Graubünden: procedure, costs, transfer tax, notary fees and how to access a sustainable mortgage loan
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - In the Canton of Graubünden, real estate purchases follow federal and cantonal regulations - The procedure requires a notary, surveyor, bank, and registration with the Land Registry Office (90-120 days) - Additional costs typically amount to 5-8% of the purchase price
## Key facts - **What**: Real estate purchase in the Canton of Graubünden - Where: Canton of Graubünden, Eastern Switzerland - Who: Buyer, notary, surveyor, bank, cantonal Land Registry Office - Timeline: 90-120 days from promise to registration - Legal basis: Code of Obligations (CO, art. 964-1004) + cantonal legislation
### How real estate purchase works in Graubünden
In the Canton of Graubünden, as in other Swiss cantons, real estate purchases follow procedures regulated by federal laws and cantonal legislation. The Swiss Code of Obligations (CO) sets the uniform legal framework, while the canton integrates with local provisions on taxation, land registry, and administrative procedures.
The process begins with a visit to the property and informal price negotiation with the seller. Once a preliminary agreement is reached, the parties proceed with the promise of sale, a formal document signed before a notary that binds both parties to their obligations. This phase is critical: the notary has the legal duty to verify the legality of the transaction, the seller's title of ownership (consulting directly the Land Registry Office of the Canton of Graubünden) and any pre-existing mortgage rights.
### Roles of the involved parties
The notary drafts the promise of sale and the final notarial deed, ensuring the transaction's compliance with regulations. In the Canton of Graubünden, as in other cantons, the notary must verify that the seller is the registered owner and that there are no liens or other encumbrances preventing the sale.
The surveyor prepares the technical appraisal of the property (planimetry, surface area, state of conservation), a document required by both the bank and the Graubünden tax authorities. The bank evaluates the property based on the appraisal and the local market, deciding the amount and conditions of the mortgage. You can compare offers from different banks through authorized platforms.
The Land Registry Office of the Canton of Graubünden manages the Land Registry, where the property and mortgage rights are registered. The registration represents the final legal act defining the transfer of ownership. Once completed, the property passes to the buyer, and the bank is secured by the registered mortgage right.
### Timelines and procedure
The overall time from the promise of sale to the final registration in the Land Registry varies from 90 to 120 days, depending on the complexity of the property, the bank's processing speed, and the local Land Registry Office's workload. For a buyer from outside the canton or abroad, it is recommended to consult a notary experienced in Graubünden law, as administrative procedures and forms vary slightly among Swiss cantons. ### Purchase costs: transfer tax, notary fees and taxes
In the Canton of Grisons, as in many Swiss cantons, the purchase of a property involves various additional costs beyond the purchase price. Real estate acquisition is one of the main components of the overall cost of living for those who decide to settle in a new region. Understanding these costs is essential to assess the overall budget and the sustainability of the investment.
The real estate transfer tax (so-called transfer tax) exists in the Canton of Grisons and is levied at the cantonal and municipal levels. The rate and calculation method vary depending on the specific municipality and the type of transfer (private sale, inheritance, etc.). The bank providing the mortgage gives an indicative estimate of this tax during the pre-approval phase of the financing.
Notary fees are set by federal law and cantonal tariffs. Generally, the cost of drafting the notarial deed corresponds to a percentage of the purchase price, calculated based on standardized tariffs. The fees of the surveyor for the technical appraisal and cadastral documentation are variable and depend on the complexity of the property.
Finally, there are registration fees with the Land Registry Office of the Canton of Grisons, necessary for the registration of the property and the mortgage. These are also modulated based on the value of the property and are relatively contained.
### Aggregate estimate of additional costs
Generally, additional costs (transfer tax, notary, surveyor, registration) range between 5% and 8% of the purchase price, depending on the Grisons municipality and the specific situation. It is therefore essential to request precise quotes from the notary and surveyor before signing any commitment.
### Tax deductibility
In Switzerland, mortgage interest is deductible from the tax return (federal and cantonal), as well as extraordinary maintenance costs of the property. In the Canton of Grisons, these deductions apply as in other cantons, following the rules of the Cantonal Tax Administration. When filling out the [annual tax return](nav:tax-return), remember to report the mortgage interest paid.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Mortgage lending and financial sustainability
The mortgage loan is the most common instrument for financing the purchase of a property in Switzerland. In the canton of Graubünden, as elsewhere, banks apply very strict sustainability criteria to evaluate the borrower's ability to repay the loan.
The golden rule of financial sustainability states that the real estate burden (mortgage installment, interest, taxes, insurance, maintenance) does not exceed 33% of the buyer's gross monthly income. This is the main criterion that banks use to approve or reject the granting of a mortgage. If the load exceeds 33%, the loan request will be rejected or reduced.
Furthermore, banks require the buyer to cover at least 20% of the purchase price with his own funds (personal savings, inheritance, pension liquidation). The remaining 80% can be financed through a mortgage loan. Some institutions allow up to 85% financing, but under more stringent conditions (higher interest rates, compulsory mortgage insurance).
### Using social security to purchase real estate
The occupational pension scheme (Second Pillar / LPP) can be partially used for the purchase of the first main residence, through the mechanism of foreclosure of pension credit. In the canton of Grisons, as well as throughout Switzerland, it is possible to withdraw up to 50% of the LPP balance (or a maximum equal to the value of the property, if lower) to reduce the mortgage and improve affordability.
Similarly, the Third Pillar (3a) can be used to finance a property that will become the primary residence. These mechanisms are particularly useful for reducing the use of large mortgages and for improving the 33% affordability rule.
### Pre-Mortgage Checklist
- Check the 33% sustainability rule (real estate burden on gross income) - Make sure you have at least 20% of your own funds - Collect the last 3 years of tax returns - Consult the bank about the possibility of using the LPP - Ask for written pre-approval before signing the promise
### Next steps
For a purchase in the Canton of Grisons, use [il nostro calcolatore](nav:calculator) to evaluate the financial sustainability of the mortgage based on your income and estimated additional costs, and consult [le banche locali](nav:banks) for the best mortgage loan offers. Once the preliminary evaluation has been completed, contact a notary or real estate agency in the Canton of Grisons directly for personalized advice.

item.title: Opening a business in Solothurn: registration and costs
item.description: Practical guide to opening a business in the canton of Solothurn: legal forms, business registration, federal/cantonal taxation and insurance obligations.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Three main legal forms (sole proprietorship, LLC, corporation) with different minimum capitals and liabilities - Registration with the commercial register within 30 days of starting operations - Taxation on three levels: federal (IFD) + cantonal (Solothurn) + municipal (variable multipliers) - Mandatory social contributions: AVS/AI 5.3% for employees, SUVA, LAMal within 3 months
## Key facts - **What**: Starting a business in the canton of Solothurn with commercial registration - When: Registration within 30 days of starting operations - Where: Solothurn cantonal commercial register office - Who: Aspiring entrepreneur residing or with a valid federal permit - Legal forms: Sole proprietorship (no minimum capital), LLC (min. CHF 20,000), Corporation (min. CHF 100,000) - AVS/AI contributions: 5.3% of employee salary; 10.6% total with employer
Starting a business in the canton of Solothurn — whether as a sole proprietorship, limited liability company (LLC), or corporation — requires compliance with precise administrative procedures and federal, cantonal, and municipal tax payments. The first step is registration with the cantonal commercial register, mandatory within 30 days of starting operations. Subsequently, tax declaration obligations and social contribution payments (AVS/AI/IPG, SUVA, LAMal, LPP if hiring employees) begin.
### Legal forms: which to choose
The choice of legal form depends on the level of personal liability you are willing to accept, the initial capital available, and the organizational complexity of the business.
The sole proprietorship is the simplest form: a single natural person, unlimited liability for commercial debts, no mandatory minimum capital. Income is taxed directly on personal assets according to IFD (direct federal tax) rules. It is the preferred choice for self-employed professionals, consultants, and small business owners.
The LLC (limited liability company) is a legal entity distinct from the owner. Minimum capital: CHF 20,000, with at least 50% paid at the time of founding. Liability is limited to the paid-in capital. Each partner holds shares and is not personally liable for business debts beyond the paid-in capital.
The corporation is suitable for medium to large-scale projects with growth potential. Minimum capital: CHF 100,000, divided into registered or bearer shares. Requires a board of directors and a shareholders' meeting. Liability for shareholders is limited to the subscribed capital.
### Registration procedure
Registration with the Solothurn cantonal commercial register is done through the cantonal commercial register office. Required documents include: valid ID, articles of association and bylaws (for corporations), simple or digitally signed declaration of business start, brief description of the activity, legal address, bank details. The registration fee varies by canton and municipality (to be verified directly with the office).
After registration, the cantonal administration automatically transmits the registration data to the Federal Customs Administration (FCA/ESTV) for VAT registration if the annual turnover exceeds CHF 100,000 in 12 consecutive months. Simultaneously, it is mandatory to register with the AVS/AI/IPG system within 5 days of hiring the first employee; if you are self-employed, registration occurs immediately. Delays in these procedures result in fines and late interest. ## Federal, cantonal, and municipal taxation
Swiss taxation follows a three-tier model. The direct federal tax (DFT), managed by the Federal Customs Administration (FCA), applies to net income and assets according to federal rates uniform across the country. In the canton of Solothurn, the cantonal tax is levied according to the canton's own rate, which varies from canton to canton. Finally, each municipality applies its own multiplier to the cantonal rate: the taxpayer pays the cantonal tax amount multiplied by the municipal coefficient. The municipal multipliers in Solothurn vary from municipality to municipality; it is essential to verify them with the Tax Office of the municipality where the activity will be conducted before starting operations.
The value-added tax (VAT), managed by the FCA, applies when the turnover exceeds CHF 100,000 in 12 consecutive months (mandatory registration), or voluntary registration can be requested if more convenient for the activity. VAT does not constitute an additional tax cost for the company but rather a periodic declaration procedure (quarterly or annual depending on the chosen regime) with the right to deduct qualified purchases.
### Social contributions: AHV, IV, EO, SUVA, LAA, LAMal
If you are the owner of a self-employed activity, you are automatically enrolled in the AHV/IV/EO system (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance, Disability Insurance; Maternity/Paternity Allowance according to federal law EO). The contributions are:
- **AHV/IV/EO**: 5.3% on the annual net income of the self-employed. If you hire employees, you pay 5.3% (employee's share) + 5.3% (employer's share) = 10.6% total on the coordinated salary. Annual coordinated maximum set annually by the Confederation (approximately CHF 149,080 in 2026, indexed every year). - Unemployment insurance (UI): 1.1% up to the annual maximum, applicable if you have employees. Employee's share + employer's share. - SUVA (workplace accidents, managed by the Swiss National Accident Insurance Institute): 0.7–1.5% of the gross salary depending on the sector of activity and the degree of risk. - LAMal (mandatory health insurance): Binding for all residents within 3 months of starting the activity. It is not a tax or a salary contribution but rather a private insurance with per capita premiums varying by canton and region. Deductibles for adults: from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 annually at choice. Cantonal subsidies available based on income. - LPP (mandatory occupational pension): If you hire employees with a coordinated salary above CHF 21,330 (2026, indexed annually), you must enroll the company in a recognized pension institution. Contribution rate varies by age bracket of the employee: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44), 15% (45–54), 18% (55+ up to the reference age). Contributions divided into employee's share/employer's share.
### Practical scenario: sole proprietorship vs. LLC
A sole proprietorship with a single owner pays self-employed AHV/IV/EO contributions (5.3% on net income). If it hires an employee with an annual gross salary of CHF 60,000, the owner continues to pay AHV/IV/EO on their own income and simultaneously pays 10.6% (AHV/IV/EO) + about 1% (UI) + 0.7–1.5% (SUVA) on the employee's salary, plus LPP if the coordinated salary exceeds CHF 21,330. An LLC with one or more partners follows the same social contribution rules for employees. The main difference is that the LLC is a legal entity separate from the owner: the owner receives dividends or profit distributions (not directly salary), subject to different federal/cantonal taxation compared to employment income.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Step-by-step procedure: from registration to first deadlines
Starting a business in the canton of Solothurn requires the orderly completion of these steps:
**1. Choose the legal form** (sole proprietorship, LLC, Corporation). If you opt for a company, consult a notary or accounting firm for the drafting of the articles of association and the bylaws (mandatory for companies).
2. Register with the commercial register of the canton of Solothurn within 30 days of the actual start of the activity. Provide: valid ID document, articles of association and bylaws (for companies), declaration of start of activity, brief description of the activity, legal address, bank details. Registration involves a cost that varies by canton and municipality (to be verified with the cantonal commercial register office).
3. Register with AVS/AI/IPG within 5 days of hiring the first employee, or immediately if you are self-employed. AVS-100 form available at the cantonal AVS office of the canton of Solothurn. Provide social security number, personal data, company data.
4. Apply for VAT registration (if the estimated turnover exceeds CHF 100,000 annually or voluntary choice). Application with the Federal Customs Administration (FCA/ESTV), form available online.
5. Register staff with SUVA/LAA and ensure accident coverage from the first day of work. Registration with SUVA (if not employed in agriculture) or LAA.
6. Take out health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of the start of operational activity. Mandatory for the owner and employees resident in Switzerland. Choose a fund from those authorized in the canton, considering the deductible and premium.
7. Periodic payments and declarations: - AVS/AI/IPG contributions: monthly by the 10th of the following month (different frequency possible by agreement). - VAT declaration: quarterly or annual according to turnover and chosen regime. - Annual tax return: by the cantonal deadline (usually March of the following year for the previous fiscal year).
### Where to find help and verify local data
Consult the [Swiss tax and contribution calculator](nav:calculator) for an accurate estimate of your federal/cantonal/municipal tax burden based on expected net income and the canton of operation. The cantonal commercial register office of Solothurn provides updated forms, detailed instructions, and direct advice for registration. The cantonal AVS office, the cantonal tax office, and the Federal Customs Administration (FCA/ESTV) are essential resources for tax declarations and payments.
Each canton and each municipality of Solothurn has its own multipliers, cantonal rates, tax breaks, and subsidies. item.description: Legal form, registration in the commercial register, cantonal taxes and social security obligations: the procedure for opening businesses in the canton of Solothurn.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Mandatory registration with the commercial register - Three levels of taxation: federal, cantonal, municipal - AVS and pension obligations if there is an employee - LAMal mandatory within 3 months, deductibles from CHF 300–2'500
## Key facts - **What**: Starting a business in the canton of Solothurn - Where: Cantonal commercial register office of Solothurn - Who: Entrepreneurs, LLCs, PLCs, sole proprietorships - Employee AVS contributions: 5.3% (10.6% total with employer) - LAMal obligations: Within 3 months of starting activity - Tax levels: Federal (IFD) + cantonal + municipal Solothurn - LPP contributions: 7–18% coordinated salary according to age - SUVA: 0.7–1.5% according to economic sector
Starting a business in the canton of Solothurn requires compliance with well-defined federal, cantonal, and municipal obligations. The Swiss tax structure is divided into three levels: the federal direct tax (IFD) is fixed at the national level, while the canton of Solothurn applies a cantonal rate and each municipality its own multiplier. This system implies that each entrepreneur is subject to cumulative taxation based on personal and business income.
Registration with the commercial register is the administrative foundation: without it, no activity can proceed legally in the canton. Simultaneously, anyone wishing to operate must activate mandatory health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of starting the activity. This obligation applies to every resident in Switzerland, including entrepreneurs, and is non-negotiable. LAMal covers health risks with deductibles ranging from CHF 300 to CHF 2'500 for adults, with individual premiums varying according to age and canton of residence. The canton of Solothurn may offer premium reductions (subsidies) based on income.
Anyone with an employee faces immediate pension obligations. The employer pays 5.3% of AVS/AI/IPG contributions for each employee (the employee in turn pays 5.3%, for a total of 10.6%). To these are added SUVA contributions (professional accident insurance, 0.7–1.5% according to the economic sector) and unemployment/professional illness insurance contributions (1.1% up to an annual maximum set at the federal level).
### Legal forms and liability
The choice of legal form — sole proprietorship, limited liability company (LLC), or public limited company (PLC) — determines civil liability, administrative complexity, and compliance burden. Sole proprietorships offer maximum operational simplicity but expose the owner to unlimited liability: in case of business debts, personal assets are at risk. LLCs and PLCs limit liability to the capital contributed, protecting the personal assets of shareholders and partners. Commercial registration is mandatory for all forms and must be completed at the competent cantonal office in Solothurn within deadlines set by federal law. The entrepreneur who opens a business in Solothurn encounters a three-tier tax structure. The direct federal tax is fixed at the national level according to federal rates. This is added to the cantonal tax of Solothurn, which applies its own rate, multiplied finally by the municipal coefficient: the result is an effective rate that varies not only between cantons but also between municipalities within the same canton. This combination generates a unique tax burden for each jurisdiction. For those with employees, the pension obligations are non-negotiable and generate a fixed personnel cost. The employer pays 5.3% of AVS/AI/IPG (the employee pays the same amount); 0.7–1.5% for SUVA depending on the sector; 1.1% for unemployment and professional health insurance up to an annual maximum. If the entrepreneur has at least one employee, they are required to contribute to professional pension provision (LPP/BVG): the employer pays a percentage of the coordinated salary that varies from 7% (25–34 age bracket) to 10% (35–44 years), 15% (45–54 years), and 18% (from 55 years until the reference age for retirement). Every resident in Switzerland — including entrepreneurs — must take out compulsory health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of arrival or starting a business. Premiums are individual and proportional to age and canton of residence, not deducted from salary but paid directly to the insurer. Deductibles for adults range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 annually. The canton of Solothurn recognizes premium reductions (cantonal subsidies) for those with low incomes, calculated according to its own criteria. ### Scenario: entrepreneur with a part-time employee Imagine a business with an owner and a part-time employee (50%). If the employee earns CHF 35,000 annually (coordinated), the employer pays approximately CHF 1,855 in AVS/AI/IPG, CHF 350 in SUVA (medium sector), CHF 385 in unemployment/occupational accident insurance, and a LPP share according to the employee's age (minimum 7%, maximum 18% of the coordinated salary). To these employment costs are added the cantonal and municipal taxes specific to the entrepreneur on income and capital, as well as personal LAMal premiums (variable according to age and chosen deductible). The total tax and insurance burden must be planned in the financial planning of startups: a common mistake is to underestimate these fixed costs. ### VAT obligations at the federal level If the annual turnover exceeds the federal threshold for mandatory VAT registration (a variable threshold updated annually by the competent federal office), the entrepreneur must register with the competent federal office and pay the value-added tax according to federal rates. Below the threshold, registration is optional but may be convenient for those with foreign clients or investors who require VAT invoices.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). The procedure to legally start a business in Solothurn follows these steps:
### Step 1 — Choosing the legal form and preparing documentation Decide between a sole proprietorship, LLC, or corporation. For corporate forms, draft the articles of association, gather identification documents (passport or ID card), obtain a criminal record certificate from the competent authorities, and appoint any managers or legal representatives.
### Step 2 — Opening a dedicated bank account At a Swiss bank, open a business account dedicated to the activity and deposit the minimum share capital required by the chosen legal form (specific amounts are determined at the federal level). The account must be in the name of the company or corporation, not the personal owner.
### Step 3 — Registration in the commercial register Submit the application to the competent cantonal office (Solothurn Canton Commercial Register), attaching the corporate documentation, the criminal record certificate, and proof of capital deposit. The process can be done online or in paper form according to cantonal procedures. Once approved, the company receives a registration number that legally identifies it.
### Step 4 — Registration as an AVS employer Simultaneously with the commercial registration, register with the competent AVS office (Solothurn Canton compensation fund) as an employer and a natural person subject to AVS. This obligation arises even if there are no employees yet, and is a prerequisite for hiring the first employee.
### Step 5 — VAT declaration (if applicable) If the annual turnover is expected to exceed the federal threshold, register with the competent federal office for VAT within the deadlines set by federal law. Registration enables billing with VAT and deducting the tax on business costs.
### Step 6 — Mandatory insurance Take out personal health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of starting the activity, with a Swiss health insurance fund. Check the canton of residence and choose the preferred deductible (CHF 300–2,500 for adults) and coverage plan. Once employees are hired, register with a SUVA fund for occupational accident insurance.
### Step 7 — Registration with a pension fund (LPP) If the company has at least one employee, choose a pension fund (BVG/LPP) registered in the Solothurn Canton register. The employer must contribute to the coordinated salary of the employee (7–18% according to age), while the employee contributes their share (typically 5–10% according to the fund's regulations).
### Critical deadlines - **Commercial register registration**: Within the deadlines set by the cantonal office after submitting the application - AVS registration: Simultaneous with commercial registration - LAMal opening: Within 3 months of starting the activity - Tax declaration: Within 60 days of the end of the fiscal year (usually by February/March) - First pay slip: With correct AVS, SUVA, LPP payments according to gross amounts
A common mistake is to underestimate the administrative times and the complexity of initial compliance. Registration in the commercial register is not the end point, but the beginning: subsequent obligations (AVS, LAMal, LPP, VAT) logically follow and must be activated precisely. Consult the [tax calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the individual tax burden according to income and canton, and the [pension portal](nav:pension) to understand the specific LPP obligations for each age group of the employee.
