## In brief - Starting a business requires choosing a legal form and registering with the Commercial Register - Taxation follows three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal — each canton has its own rates - Pension (AVS/LPP) and insurance (LAMal, SUVA) obligations are mandatory for businesses and employees
## Key facts - **What**: Procedure for starting an economic activity with different legal forms - Where: Canton of Solothurn - Who: Owner, self-employed, company - Form: Sole proprietorship, SA, Sarl, simple partnership - Register: Mandatory registration with the cantonal Commercial Register - Taxes: Three levels — federal (IFD), cantonal, municipal
--- Starting a business in the Canton of Solothurn requires compliance with administrative, tax, and pension obligations at three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal. Choosing the legal form is the first decisive step.
### Legal forms: sole proprietorship, public limited company, limited liability company In Switzerland, the entrepreneur chooses between a sole proprietorship (no legal personality, unlimited liability), simple partnership, limited partnership, public limited company (SA) or limited liability company (Sarl). Each form entails substantial differences: a sole proprietorship does not require minimum capital; an Sarl requires at least CHF 20,000 and is a company with legal personality; an SA requires at least CHF 100,000. The choice depends on the nature of the activity, the expected turnover, and the personal risk tolerance.
### Registration with the Commercial Register Registration with the Commercial Register of the Canton of Solothurn is mandatory to operate a commercial or craft business. This public register centralizes the legal identity of the company, the owner, the headquarters, and the legal form. The cantonal administration or the delegated municipal authority manages the registration and issues the trade certificate, a fundamental document for operating legally.
### The three levels of taxation: federal, cantonal, municipal The company becomes a taxable entity at three independent tax levels. The federal direct tax (IFD) is calculated by the Federal Tax Administration (FTA) on the net income. The cantonal tax of the Canton of Solothurn follows local cantonal regulations. The municipal tax is determined by the municipal multiplier applied to the cantonal taxable income. This system implies that the same income is subject to three successive taxations.
### Pension and insurance obligations: AVS, LPP, LAMal, SUVA The company registers with the pension authorities. For each employee, contributions to AVS (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance) and AI (Disability Insurance) are mandatory. If the coordinated salary exceeds the federal threshold, professional pension (LPP) is mandatory. The sole proprietor pays AVS contributions independently. Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for residents. Accident insurance (SUVA) is mandatory if the company has employees. ### Taxes on three levels
Swiss taxation is not centralized in a single federal rate. The Soletta company will pay three separate taxes: the federal direct tax (IFD) calculated by the Federal Tax Administration (FTA), the cantonal tax determined by the Canton of Soletta with its own rates, and the municipal tax calculated on the cantonal income multiplied by the municipal multiplier. Each level has separate deadlines, calculation methods, and payment offices. A single company submits three annual declarations and receives three tax assessments. This three-tier system is stable in all Swiss cantons: no canton has a centralized taxation system.
### Pension obligations: AVS, AI, LPP
For each employee hired, the employer is required to pay contributions to the Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (AVS) and the Disability Insurance (AI). The employee's share is 5.3% of the gross salary, while the employer pays their share of 5.3%, for a total of 10.6%. The contributions are mandatory and paid to the Soletta Cantonal Pension Fund or an authorized private fund.
Professional Pension (LPP) is mandatory if the coordinated salary (gross salary minus a federal deduction) exceeds the normed minimum. LPP contributions vary according to the insured's age: the employer contributes from 7% to 18% of the coordinated salary, depending on the employee's age class. Additionally, the owner of a sole proprietorship pays AVS contributions on themselves — not from the salary, but on an independent contribution base calculated on net income. This payment is optional if the activity is secondary, mandatory if it is primary.
### Health insurance and liability insurance
Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for every resident in Switzerland. It is not a salary contribution, but a private policy with a per capita premium: the owner and employees must subscribe to it within three months of starting the activity. The deductibles for adults range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 at the insured's choice. LAMal does not cover occupational accidents (competence of SUVA) nor dental care, except for optional coverages. Accident insurance (SUVA or equivalent mutual entity) is mandatory if the company has employees and covers injuries and occupational diseases; the contribution varies by sector of activity.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Operational procedure: step by step
The procedure to start a business in the Canton of Solothurn follows a well-defined administrative sequence, to be completed according to specific deadlines.
Phase 1: Choice of legal form — Consult a tax advisor or lawyer to evaluate which legal form (sole proprietorship, LLC, Corporation) is most suitable for the type of activity, available capital, and desired liability. Each form has different tax, accounting, and organizational implications.
Phase 2: Opening a bank account — Before registering with the Commercial Register, open a business account with a Swiss bank. Banks require documentation on the legal form, the articles of association (for companies), and the owner's data.
Phase 3: Registration with the Commercial Register — Contact the Commercial Register office of the Canton of Solothurn at the cantonal administration or the delegated municipal authority. Complete the official registration form and attach documents: certificate of previous trade (if any), identity document, articles of association (for companies). Registration is mandatory; without it, it is not lawful to carry out the activity.
Phase 4: Registration with the AFC — After registration with the Commercial Register, the VAT number/AFC customer number is automatically assigned or upon request. This number is essential for invoicing, VAT obligations, and communication with the Federal Tax Administration.
Phase 5: Registration with social security — Register with the cantonal social security institute of the Canton of Solothurn (or with an authorized private fund) for the employees' AHV/IV. The employer receives an affiliation number and a communication of the payment deadlines (usually monthly or quarterly).
**Phase 6: Health insurance** — Subscribe to a LAMal policy with a Swiss health insurance fund within three months of starting the activity.
Phase 7: Accident insurance — If the company has employees, conclude an accident insurance contract with SUVA or an equivalent mutual insurance company.
### Administrative deadlines and payments
The federal tax return must be submitted to the AFC by the federal deadline (usually March-April of the following year). The Canton of Solothurn and the municipalities set their own deadlines for the cantonal and municipal declarations. The tax installments are communicated following the initial declaration and paid on annual dates set by the administrations.
Social security contributions (AHV/IV/LPP) are paid monthly or quarterly, depending on the agreement with the pension fund. Late payments incur interest and administrative penalties. Always consult local tax advisors in the Canton of Solothurn, who know the specific cantonal and municipal regulations and can guide the entrepreneur through all deadlines and payments.
To estimate the federal, cantonal, and municipal tax burden of your company, it is useful to use [tax and salary calculation tools](nav:calculator). Tax and social security planning advice helps optimize the company structure and payments. To learn more about [professional pension and AHV/LPP obligations](nav:pension), consult the cantonal social security institute of Solothurn directly.

item.title: Opening a business in Solothurn: costs and procedures
item.description: From legal forms to the costs of registration in the commercial register, insurance obligations: how to start a business in the Canton of Soletta.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Four legal forms available: sole proprietorship, LLC, Corporation, cooperative - Mandatory registration with the federal commercial register, centralized procedure - Minimum capital CHF 20'000 for Corporation and LLC (at least half paid before registration) - Federal insurance obligations: AHV/AI/IPG, LAMal, LAINF, LPP
## Key facts - **What**: Opening and registering activities in the Canton of Solothurn - Where: Swiss federal commercial register (managed by the cantons) - Who: Swiss citizens, permanent residents, foreigners with work permit - Legal forms: Sole proprietorship, LLC, Corporation, cooperative - Minimum capital: CHF 20'000 for Corporation and LLC - AHV/AI/IPG contributions: 5.3% employee (10.6% total with employer) - Maximum hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices, sales) or 50 hours other sectors - LAMal: Mandatory insurance for residents within 3 months of arrival
Opening a business in the Canton of Solothurn means navigating a federal and cantonal administrative system with uniform national regulations. Switzerland does not have a federal minimum wage — some cantons have their own — but requires registration with the federal commercial register, choice of legal form, and compliance with mandatory insurance and tax obligations.
### The four legal forms
The choice of legal structure is the first critical step. Each form has different implications for liability, taxation, and administrative complexity.
The sole proprietorship is the simplest form: the entrepreneur is a natural person, with unlimited liability for business debts. It does not require minimum capital, but personal assets remain exposed. Ideal for freelancers and professionals who want reduced initial costs.
The Limited Liability Company (LLC, or GmbH/Sàrl in other regions) limits liability to the paid-in capital. Minimum capital CHF 20'000: at least half (CHF 10'000) must be deposited in a Swiss bank before registration, the rest within 5 years. Requires at least one shareholder. It is the preferred structure for small and medium-sized businesses.
The Corporation (Corp, or AG/SA) also has a minimum capital of CHF 20'000 and limited liability, but requires more complex administrative structures: bylaws, shareholders' meeting, board of directors. Suitable for medium to large businesses.
The cooperative operates with a minimum number of members varying by canton. Each member has an equal right to vote. Common in the agricultural, craft, and commercial sectors.
### Registration with the federal commercial register
Registration with the commercial register is mandatory before starting activities. The procedure is centralized at the federal level to ensure legal uniformity throughout Switzerland. Each canton manages the competent commercial register office, which collects applications and transmits them to the federal register.
Required documents vary by legal form: for a sole proprietorship, personal data and activity description are sufficient; for capital companies, bylaws, bank deposit documents, list of shareholders are needed. Processing times: approximately 2-4 weeks after submitting complete documentation. Once registered, the company receives a nationally valid business number. ### Minimum capital and registration fees
The minimum capital thresholds are set at the federal level for legal uniformity, but the registration fees for the commercial register are managed by the cantons, so they vary.
For a limited liability company, the minimum capital is CHF 20,000. At least half (CHF 10,000) must be deposited in a Swiss bank before registration. The remainder can be paid within 5 years without penalty, provided it is paid according to the company's regulations.
For a joint-stock company, the minimum capital is identical: CHF 20,000. Half must be deposited before registration.
A sole proprietorship has no mandatory minimum capital, making it a low initial cost option.
The registration fees for the commercial register in the Canton of Solothurn vary according to the legal form and the declared capital. It is advisable to contact the Solothurn Canton Commercial Register Office directly for exact amounts and updated procedures, as the rates can be reviewed annually.
### The three-tier tax system
Anyone opening a business in Switzerland faces a tax burden determined by three levels of government:
**Federal level**: Federal direct tax (FDT) on individuals or business profits. Managed by the Federal Customs Administration. The rate is progressive and varies with income.
Canton level: Cantonal income and capital tax. In the Canton of Solothurn, it is managed by the cantonal administration. Rates vary significantly among Swiss cantons.
Municipal level: Multiplier applied to the cantonal tax. Each municipality applies its own multiplier, making the final rate variable even within the same canton of Solothurn. A common multiplier of 1.5 means that the cantonal tax is multiplied by 1.5 at the municipal level.
For a sole proprietorship, the income is taxed as personal income at the three levels. For capital companies (SA, SARL), the profit is taxed at the business level (profit taxes), and then the dividends distributed to shareholders are taxed again at the personal level. The total tax burden on a business can vary from 25% to 35% of gross income depending on the chosen legal form and specific location.
### AVS/AI/IPG registration obligations for employees
Anyone hiring employees must register the company with the competent AVS/AI/IPG compensation fund for the payment of mandatory contributions. Insured employees pay 5.3% of gross salary (AVS/AI/IPG combined, including unemployment risk). The employer pays a total of 10.6% (5.3% employee + 5.3% employer).
This registration is separate from the commercial register registration and must be done within 30 days of hiring the first employee. Delay in paying contributions exposes the company to fines and retroactive recovery.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Federal and cantonal insurance obligations
Anyone starting a business and hiring employees must comply with mandatory federal insurance obligations.
**Health insurance (LAMal)**: Mandatory for all residents in Switzerland within 3 months of arrival. Premiums are private, per capita, and not deductible as salary contributions. Adult deductibles range from CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500. Each canton offers premium reductions (subsidies) based on income bracket. In the Canton of Solothurn, subsidies are managed by the cantonal administration.
AVS/AI/IPG (mandatory pension): For each employee, the employer contributes 5.3% (matching the employee's 5.3%). The total amount is 10.6% of gross salary. Included: AVS 2.2% (employee) + AI 0.7% (employee) + IPG 0.5% (employee) + Unemployment reserve 1.1% (employee) + identical percentages for the employer.
Accident insurance (LAINF/LAA): Mandatory if employees are hired for more than 8 hours per week. The rate varies by economic sector: 0.7–1.5% of gross salary. For high-risk sectors, the rate is higher. Managed by SUVA or authorized private insurers.
Unemployment insurance (AD/AC): Mandatory for employees with a salary above a minimum threshold. Total contribution 1.1% up to an annual maximum. Employee and employer pay equal shares.
Professional pension (LPP/BVG): Mandatory for employees with a coordinated salary ≥CHF 22,050 annually (figure indexed each year). Contribution rates vary by age bracket: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44 years), 15% (45–54 years), 18% (55+ years up to the reference age). Managed by authorized pension funds.
### Step-by-step procedure to start a business
Step 1: Choose the legal form most suitable for your business model (sole proprietorship, LLC, corporation, cooperative).
Step 2: If LLC or corporation, deposit the minimum capital (at least half of CHF 20,000) in a Swiss bank and obtain a deposit certificate.
Step 3: Register with the federal commercial register. Contact the Commercial Register Office of the Canton of Solothurn and submit complete documentation (articles of association for companies, identity document, list of shareholders, bank certificate, activity description).
Step 4: Wait for approval (approximately 2-4 weeks). Once registered, you will receive a nationally valid business number.
Step 5: Register with the competent AVS/AI/IPG compensation fund for the Canton of Solothurn, providing the business number and employee details. This must be done within 30 days of hiring the first employee.
Step 6: If not already insured, take out LAMal within 3 months of arrival (for residents). Contact a health insurance fund in your canton and choose the deductible model.
Step 7: If you hire employees, register for LAINF/LAA with SUVA or an authorized private insurer, providing the business number and activity description.
Step 8: If the expected turnover exceeds CHF 100,000 annually, register for VAT with the Federal Customs Administration. The standard VAT rate is 7.7%.
Step 9: Open a business bank account with a Swiss bank to separate personal and business funds.
Step 10: Declare the start of the business to the tax administration of the Canton of Solothurn for cantonal and municipal taxation.
### Planning the initial budget
To calculate the tax burden (IFD, cantonal and municipal tax), AVS/AI/IPG contributions, LAMal, and other insurance costs, use [our salary calculator](nav:calculator). If you plan to hire employees, the tool also shows the total labor cost. For in-depth pension planning beyond AVS/AI/IPG, consult the guide on [professional pension](nav:pension). If you have questions about the [annual tax return](nav:tax-return), our national portal offers forms and clarifications for entrepreneurs.

## In brief - The Solothurn compensation fund links the federal AVS and local cantonal benefits - AVS contributions paid: 5.3% on salary (employee), 5.3% (employer) - Contribution gaps directly reduce the monthly pension amount - Supplementary benefits bridge the gap to the cantonal minimum living standard
## Key facts - **What**: Cantonal pension system in the Canton of Solothurn (first pillar AVS + supplementary benefits) - When: Continuous during affiliation and in retirement - Where: Canton of Solothurn, Switzerland - Who: Solothurn cantonal compensation fund, AVS affiliates, retirees - Amount: Contributions 5.3% employee + 5.3% employer for AVS - Authority: Solothurn cantonal compensation fund
### The first pillar in the Canton of Solothurn
In the Canton of Solothurn, as in all of Switzerland, old-age pensions are based on three pillars. The first pillar is the AVS (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance), which is mandatory for all employed and self-employed workers. It is managed at the federal level with the essential coordination of the cantonal compensation fund, which acts as a link between local affiliates and the national system.
The Solothurn compensation fund performs crucial functions: it collects monthly contributions from salaries (5.3% paid by the employee, 5.3% by the employer for AVS, plus AI), records each payment in the personal history of each affiliate, and at the time of retirement calculates the pension based on the complete contribution history. The link with supplementary benefits is essential: when AVS and disability insurance (AI) do not reach the cantonal minimum living standard, supplementary benefits intervene to cover the gap.
Those who have regularly paid contributions during their working life receive an old-age pension calculated on a precise formula: years of affiliation multiplied by the average recorded income. However, it is not that simple. Any contribution gaps — periods in which nothing was paid due to illness, unemployment, family care, or other reasons — directly reduce the monthly pension amount. This is where supplementary benefits (PC) come in: a cantonal mechanism that checks whether the sum of AVS and AI falls below the minimum living standard defined in Solothurn, and if so, supplements it to that level.
For those living or working in Solothurn, using the [salary calculator](/nav:calculator) helps to understand how much is being paid annually in contributions and how much is accumulated over time towards the future pension. ### Calculation of the AVS pension and the impact of contribution gaps
The AVS pension is not a fixed amount: it depends entirely on the years of contributions paid. In Switzerland, you must have at least one year of contributions to be entitled to a pension, even a minimal one. The system takes into account all the years of affiliation from the beginning of working life (around 17 years) until the retirement age set by federal law.
Each year of regularly paid contributions progressively "fills" the personal contribution history. If entire years are missing (gaps), the pension amount decreases proportionally. A gap does not mean losing the pension entirely but receiving a significantly lower amount compared to someone with a complete contribution history.
The compensation fund of Solothurn manages this critical verification: it collects monthly contributions from employees and employers, records them in the personal history, checks for any registration gaps, and at the time of retirement, calculates the total accumulated contribution amount. This amount is then converted into a monthly pension using official federal conversion tables, which also take into account life expectancy.
An often underestimated aspect: gaps are not always "total losses." Some periods are automatically covered by solidarity contributions — for example, periods when unemployment benefits were received (Unemployment automatically pays contributions) or recognized social benefits. Checking the individual account statement with the compensation fund is the first step to identifying real gaps and not registration errors.
### Supplementary benefits: the role in the Canton of Solothurn
If the sum of AVS + AI falls below the cantonal minimum living standard, supplementary benefits automatically intervene (provided an application is submitted). The minimum living standard is not a federal value equal everywhere: each canton defines it based on the local cost of living, average rents, and basic needs for a dignified life. In Solothurn, as in other cantons, this level is periodically reviewed to adapt to inflation.
Those who receive an AVS pension below the minimum living standard — a frequent situation if there are significant contribution gaps, if contributions were started relatively late, or if there were long periods of unemployment — can apply for supplementary benefits. The procedure requires submitting an official application to the canton or the municipality of residence, with documentation of the financial situation, income, actual rents paid, and other relevant expenses (e.g., health insurance premiums, continuous medical care).
Once the application is received, the competent office performs a verification: it calculates the minimum living standard of your municipality, subtracts the sum of AVS + AI, and if there is a gap, approves a permanent monthly subsidy until that level is reached. The subsidy is a right guaranteed by cantonal law, not a gratuity. Consulting [pension calculations](/nav:pension) helps estimate your expected income.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to verify your contributions and access complementary services
The first fundamental step for those who live or work in the Soletta is to check their personal contribution history. All AVS affiliates have the right to consult the individual account statement at the cantonal clearing house of Solothurn or through a federal online portal. This document shows year by year exactly what contributions were paid and what taxable income was recorded with each employer.
It is crucial to check that there are no unjustified gaps or administrative errors. If you discover an unexplained gap — for example, a period of work in which no contributions are found — you can ask the cashier for detailed information about what happened. Some gaps are covered retroactively if it is shown that you were in occupational illness, subsidized unemployment, or other protected status at that time. Other gaps can be filled if there is evidence of unrecorded wages.
When approaching the standard retirement age (65 years in the Soleta), the system automatically sends an official communication with a preliminary estimate of the monthly pension. If this estimate is lower than the cantonal minimum living allowance, the fund informs at the same time about the possibility of submitting an application for supplementary benefits already before retiring.

item.title: The Swiss have never earned and saved as much as they do today
item.description: For the first time, disposable income exceeds CHF 65,000 and the voluntary savings rate is 19.3%. The UST data confirms the historical record.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Corrected disposable income 2025: 65'124 francs, first time above 65'000 - Voluntary savings rate at 19.3%, double that of 30 years ago - Growth since 1995: +36% net of inflation
## Key facts - **What**: Corrected disposable income and savings behavior of Swiss households - When: Data updated to 2025, published Tuesday by the Federal Statistical Office - Where: All of Switzerland (national average) - Who: Federal Statistical Office (FSO) - Disposable income 2025: 65'124 francs per inhabitant - Voluntary savings 2025: 19.3% of corrected gross disposable income - Growth 1995-2025: +36% net of inflation
For the first time in modern history, the corrected disposable income of Swiss residents has exceeded the 65'000 franc mark per inhabitant. In 2025, according to data published Tuesday by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), this indicator reached 65'124 francs, representing the highest level in the entire available historical series.
Even more significant is the behavior regarding earned money. The voluntary savings rate of Swiss households has reached 19.3%, almost double the 9.7% recorded thirty years earlier. It is the highest value ever recorded in Switzerland.
Over the past three decades, corrected disposable income per inhabitant has grown steadily. Net of inflation, the growth between 1995 (when it was 40'083 francs) and 2025 corresponds to almost 36%. The average purchasing power of Swiss residents today is therefore much higher than that of a generation ago.
The growth of the overall savings rate has been even more pronounced. In 1995 it was at 19.6%, while in 2025 it reached 27.4%. This means that more than a quarter of the resources available to families is set aside as savings.
### A long-term trend
Over the last thirty years, corrected disposable income per inhabitant has grown steadily, as confirmed by FSO data. However, this snapshot describes a national average and should not make us forget the existing differences between regions, income brackets, and types of households. The increase in housing costs, health insurance premiums, and other mandatory expenses continues to weigh on many families.
Looking at the entire population, the long-term trend is nevertheless clear: Swiss families have never been so financially sound. ### The role of the pandemic and the change in behavior
The propensity to save has followed an interesting path over the last few decades. After a phase of moderate growth between the late 1990s and the first decade of the 2000s, the propensity to save began to strengthen gradually. But the real turning point came during the pandemic, when restrictions on consumption significantly increased household savings.
What is surprising, however, is that once the health emergency ended, there was no return to previous values. On the contrary: savings continued to increase significantly. This is a sign of financial capacity that has consolidated over the years and was not temporarily due solely to restrictions.
Translated into concrete numbers: every person living in Switzerland in 2025 spent about 53,000 francs and saved nearly 18,000 francs, of which about 12,600 francs in the form of voluntary savings. These are figures that reflect widespread economic solidity, although the differences between regions and social categories remain significant.
### Mandatory costs and regional disparities
The overall picture of well-being hides complexities. Swiss households not only earn more but also have greater margins to accumulate wealth, deal with unexpected events, and plan for the future. The growth of well-being appears more marked than suggested by the mere increase in income.
However, this portrait describes a national average and erases the concrete difficulties of many families. The increase in housing costs, health insurance premiums, and other mandatory expenses continues to represent a significant burden on many households. The differences between regions and social categories remain marked, and not all Swiss people benefit equally from the increase in average disposable income.
The increasing availability of resources to be allocated to savings means that families can better cope with the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) in Switzerland, especially for essential items such as rents and health insurance premiums. With greater savings capacity, it is appropriate to evaluate one's long-term financial strategy and one's [pension planning](nav:pension).

item.description: How to become a Swiss citizen in Solothurn: years of residence, language and integration tests, municipal taxes and process times.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Permit C + 10 years of residence: federal basis - Solothurn has specific language and integration criteria - Language test and administrative checks are mandatory - Municipal and cantonal taxes vary by territory
## Key facts - **What**: Ordinary naturalization to become a Swiss citizen - Where: Canton of Solothurn and municipalities of northwestern Switzerland - Federal requirement: Residence permit (C) + 10 years of residence - Who manages: SEM (State Secretariat for Migration), cantonal administration, municipalities - Procedures: Language test, integration, security checks
Naturalization in the Canton of Solothurn represents the path through which a foreign resident acquires Swiss citizenship and gains full political and civil rights. The process is governed by three normative levels: federal law, Solothurn cantonal provisions, and local municipal procedures. At the federal level, the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) establishes migration criteria, while the Canton of Solothurn and its municipalities apply additional integration and administrative verification requirements.
One of the fundamental prerequisites is the possession of a residence permit, category C, which represents the most stable residence title available for foreigners in Switzerland. At the federal level, this permit is normally granted after ten years of continuous residence. In certain contexts, the years between the second and seventh year of residence can count as double towards reaching the ten-year threshold if the applicant has demonstrated solid professional and social integration.
### Cantonal and municipal requirements
Once the permit C is acquired, the candidate must meet the specific criteria of the Canton of Solothurn. These include a demonstration of knowledge of the local language (German) and a mastery of the fundamental principles and values of Switzerland. Additionally, the municipality of residence conducts administrative and security checks to ensure that the applicant does not have significant criminal records or compliance issues with Swiss laws.
The procedure is coordinated between the three administrative levels. The SEM verifies the national migration profile, the Canton of Solothurn manages the specific linguistic and cultural integration criteria of that region, and the local municipality conducts the administrative checks and communicates the final outcome. The time required to complete the procedure generally takes months, depending on the completeness of the submitted documentation and the workload of the municipal and cantonal offices. ### Practical implications of naturalization
Once Swiss citizenship has been acquired in the Canton of Solothurn, the new citizen gains access to rights previously inaccessible as a foreign resident. At the federal level, Switzerland practices direct democracy with four voting dates per year for federal consultations: the new citizen acquires the right to participate in these votes and in the cantonal and municipal votes of Solothurn. Additionally, they can sign a popular initiative (which requires 100,000 signatures in 18 months) or contribute to an optional referendum (which requires 50,000 signatures in 100 days).
From an economic and professional standpoint, Swiss citizenship removes any professional restrictions related to migratory status. A new Swiss citizen in Solothurn gains unrestricted access to the [national job market](nav:jobs), public competitions, and regulated professions. Additionally, they gain access to the complete social security system without temporal contribution constraints.
### Step-by-step: what to do
Before submitting the naturalization application at the municipal level, the candidate must verify that they possess a valid C permit from the SEM, accumulate the ten years of residence required by federal law, and gather documents of linguistic integration such as language certificates and work references. Subsequently, they must obtain a declaration of absence of security problems from the Canton of Solothurn, complete the application form of the municipality of residence, and submit the entire documentation to the competent municipal office.
The candidate's dossier is then subjected to administrative review by the municipality, then by the Canton of Solothurn, and finally by the SEM for the final federal approval. Throughout this period, the candidate remains the holder of the C permit and can continue to live and work normally in Switzerland.
### Differences between cantons
Although federal law imposes ten years of residence for all cantons, the criteria for linguistic integration and cultural requirements vary significantly between regions. A canton in Romandy requires French, one in German-speaking Switzerland requires German, and Ticino requires Italian. Similarly, the level of rigor of security checks and the minimum number of years of absence from legal problems differ by municipality and canton. Solothurn, being in the northwest German-speaking area, has specific language and integration requirements adapted to that linguistic community.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Where to go and required documents
The first point of contact is the population office (Einwohneramt) or the municipal integration office in your municipality of residence in Solothurn. There you can request an information meeting to verify if you meet the preliminary residence requirements and if your administrative situation is in order. The municipal office will provide you with an exact list of the required documentation and guide you through the next steps.
Typically required documents include a residence certificate or extract from the municipal registers documenting 10 years of continuity, valid identification documents (passport, ID card), language certificates for Swiss German (TELC, GOETHE diplomas or equivalents), a certificate of no criminal record requested by the Swiss authorities, socio-professional integration certificates (employer references, letters of recommendation), and the naturalization application form provided by the municipality.
### Timelines and deadlines
Submitting the application to the municipality is the first formal step. Once submitted, the file moves to the Canton of Solothurn for the evaluation of integration criteria, then to the SEM at the federal level. The entire procedure from the municipal application to federal approval generally takes several weeks or months, depending on the completeness of the file and the administrative workload. Once naturalization is approved, the municipality of residence issues the Swiss citizenship certificate. This document is the legal basis for renewing the Swiss passport at the federal passport offices.
### How to use our tools
If you have questions about income tax during the residence period in Switzerland before naturalization, our [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) helps you plan your finances and understand federal, cantonal, and municipal tax deductions. Additionally, to understand how Swiss citizenship affects your pension rights (AVS and LPP), consult our [guide to the Swiss pension system](nav:pension). For further legal and procedural details specific to Solothurn, contact the municipal office or the Canton of Solothurn directly through their institutional websites. The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) also provides a general information page on ordinary naturalization on the admin.ch portal.

item.description: Matteo Buzzi, a Verdi MP, criticises the UDC initiative on armed neutrality. It proposes nonviolent civil defense instead of rearmament.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell -Member Verdi Buzzi criticizes UDC initiative on armed neutrality in the Constitution - Proposes unarmed civil defense instead of military rearmament - Calls for a NO vote on the federal initiative
## Key facts - **Who**: Matteo Buzzi, Verdi MP, Gran Consiglio, Locarno - What: Critical UDC initiative on armed neutrality in the Constitution (paragraph 1) - Historical: Initiatives "For a Switzerland without an army" in 1989 and 2001 - Proposal: Non-armed and non-violent civil defence, international cooperation - Territory: Swiss Federal Initiative, national impact
Matteo Buzzi, deputy of the Greens in the Grand Council in Locarno, accuses the Democratic Union of the Centre of betraying Swiss pacifism. The UDC initiative introduces the concept of 'armed neutrality' in paragraph 1 of the Constitution. A choice, according to Buzzi, that goes in the opposite direction from the traditional pacifism that has characterized the Swiss movement for decades.
True pacifism is not defended with weapons. For decades, the Swiss peace movement has pursued a clear idea: a Switzerland without an army, capable of building its security on cooperation, international law, solidarity between peoples and non-violent civil defence. Those who voted for the "For a Switzerland without an army" initiatives in 1989 and 2001 did so precisely for this reason — not rifles, missiles, cannons and combat aircraft, but disarmament, diplomacy and non-violent instruments.
The initiative A radically different model emerges from Buzzi's proposal: a non-armed and non-violent civil defense. It is not a new vision. In Italy, it has been discussed for some time, from the insights of Aldo Capitini and Alexander Langer to the 'Civil Peace Corps' and proposals for a Non-Armed and Non-Violent Civil Defense, oriented towards preventing conflicts and protecting populations without resorting to weapons.

The choice between armed neutrality and pacifist neutrality is not abstract. ### What armed neutrality would mean
If the UDC initiative were to pass, the Constitution would crystallize the concept of armed neutrality as a fundamental principle of the State. This would not mean an immediate change in spending, but establishes an ideological anchor that would further foster a spiral of rearmament. Buzzi points out that the UDC is already the main supporter of the ongoing rearmament, which absorbs huge financial resources. These resources could instead be invested in diplomacy, international cooperation and solidarity programmes towards countries in conflict, reducing Switzerland's vulnerability to geopolitical pressures.
### The civil defense model
The pacifist alternative is not the absence of defence, but 'different defence': defence through civil and non-violent means. Buzzi cites the model of Unarmed and Nonviolent Civil Defense, which has been debated for decades in Italy and internationally. Pay the fees: Families must pay the fees calculated based on family income. Cantonal subsidies can cover a significant portion of the costs, reducing the financial burden. 4. Start childcare: Once the registration procedure and payment of fees are completed, children can start benefiting from the assistance.
### Useful Tools For further information and to register, families can visit the website of the competent authority or contact the childcare facilities directly. Additionally, online tools are available to calculate the fees and available subsidies, making the procedure even simpler and more transparent.
### Conclusion Childcare in the Canton of Solothurn offers a convenient and accessible solution for working families. With a variety of options available and fees calculated based on income, families can find the assistance they need without facing excessive financial burden. Furthermore, cantonal subsidies make the assistance even more accessible, ensuring that all children can benefit from quality care.
For further information and to register, families can visit the website of the competent authority or contact the childcare facilities directly.

item.title: How to find an internship in the Canton of Graubünden
item.description: Guide to vocational training in Graubünden: internship contracts, apprentice remuneration, social contributions and professional maturity in the Swiss system.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Swiss dual training alternates between company practice and vocational school - In Graubünden, federal and cantonal regulations are coordinated - The apprenticeship contract is binding and protected by law - Berufsmaturität allows access to SUP after apprenticeship
## Key facts - **What**: Dual vocational training path (practice + school) - Where: Canton of Graubünden, Switzerland - Who: Apprentices, companies, cantonal vocational training office - Duration: Typically 3-4 years per sector - Social contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% (split between apprentice and company)
In the canton of Graubünden, as in the rest of Switzerland, dual vocational training is one of the three pillars of the educational system. An apprentice alternates between company practice and vocational school, developing specific skills for the job market. In Switzerland, over 60% of young people choose vocational training over the high school path.
The vocational training office of the canton of Graubünden coordinates the offer of apprenticeship positions, manages apprenticeship contracts, and recognizes diplomas. Each company that wants to train apprentices must comply with federal laws and specific cantonal ordinances for the sector. The path is regulated by the federal law on vocational training and sectoral ordinances, which define duration, programs, quality standards, and minimum salaries per year of apprenticeship.
The apprenticeship contract is a binding legal instrument that protects both the apprentice and the company, defining rights, duties, hours, holidays, and salary. The professional maturity (Berufsmaturität) is an opportunity for those who want to continue higher education after or in parallel with the apprenticeship, guaranteeing access to professional universities (SUP).
### The vocational training system in Graubünden
In Graubünden, three levels of governance operate. The Confederation sets federal standards through law. The canton defines sectoral ordinances, manages apprentice registers, and supervises training companies. Individual companies sign the apprenticeship contract, which is the legal basis of the relationship.
A critical aspect: Switzerland does not have a federal minimum wage (some cantons have their own). In Graubünden, the apprentice's salary is agreed upon in the contract and must respect the minimums indicated by the federal sectoral ordinance for the professional branch. Typically, a first-year apprentice earns less than a third-year apprentice, in proportion to their professional development and productivity.
Social contributions start from the first euro earned. The company and the apprentice split the AVS/AI/IPG contribution at 5.3% each, paid monthly to the compensation fund. Additionally, the company pays LAINF contributions (work accident insurance, 0.7-1.5% depending on the sector) and, if applicable, AD/AC (unemployment, 1.1% up to the annual maximum). These contributions protect the apprentice in case of injury, disability, or job loss. ### Internship contract: contents and legal protections
The internship contract is a legal document that must contain: the name and address of the company and the apprentice; the start and end date of the internship (total duration); the profession and number of the federal sectoral ordinance; the weekly working hours; the monthly salary for each year of the internship; holidays (minimum 4 weeks per year; 5 if the apprentice is under 20 years old); vocational school courses (usually 1-2 days per week); termination conditions; probation period provisions.
The contract is registered with the professional training office of the canton of Graubünden, which verifies compliance with federal and cantonal laws. Both the apprentice and the company receive a countersigned copy. The office rejects defective contracts and requests corrections before registration.
### Salary and tax declarations
The apprentice's salary is subject to cantonal and municipal taxes according to the rates of Graubünden. The federal direct tax (FDT) is progressive and calculated on the total annual income. Switzerland applies a three-level system (federal + cantonal + municipal); each municipality has its own multiplier on the cantonal tax.
The company pays the apprentice's AVS/AI/IPG contributions to the compensation fund (CAA) monthly. The apprentice receives a gross salary, from which insurance contributions and taxes are deducted. The net amount depends on the agreed salary, mandatory social contributions, and the tax rates of the municipality of residence.
Practical scenario: A first-year apprentice pays AVS/AI/IPG contributions at 5.3%, while the company pays its counterpart by paying the total (10.6%) to the CAA. The final net amount depends on the deductions for cantonal and municipal taxes of Graubünden. Each municipality has autonomy in setting the multiplier on the cantonal tax, so two apprentices with the same gross salary in different municipalities of Graubünden may receive slightly different net amounts.
### Health insurance and social protection
The apprentice must insure themselves with a cantonal health insurance fund within 3 months of the start of the internship. The **LAMal** (mandatory health insurance) is not a tax or salary contribution: it is a private insurance with per capita premiums varying by canton and age group. Graubünden, like every canton, offers premium subsidies (premium reduction) for those with low income and proven need.
Accident insurance (LAINF/LAA) is automatically covered by the company without additional costs for the apprentice during work activities. Accidents during the journey to and from vocational school are covered up to certain limits. Old-age provision (LPP/BVG) begins if the annual salary exceeds a coordination threshold set at the federal level (not yet specified in the brief).
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to find an internship: step-by-step guide
#### Step 1: Consult the official cantonal portal
The professional training office of the canton of Graubünden maintains a public register of available internship positions, also accessible through national [job portals](nav:jobs). Companies report vacant positions, which are published online with filters for sector, municipality, and start year. The search is free and accessible to all interested parties.
#### Step 2: Apply directly to companies
It is not mandatory to wait for an official announcement. Many companies accept spontaneous applications. It is recommended to contact the human resources office or the training manager directly, sending a CV, cover letter, and school results. Companies intending to train apprentices have specific criteria for selection and access.
#### Step 3: Draw up the contract and registration
Once an agreement is reached with a company, the internship contract is drafted. The company has official models provided by the canton. The contract must be signed by both parties and sent to the professional training office at least 2 weeks before the start of the internship. If the contract does not meet federal or cantonal requirements, the office rejects it and requests corrections. Once approved, the office officially registers the internship and communicates the data to the compensation fund.
#### Step 4: Enroll in the vocational school
Based on the registered contract, the apprentice receives an official notice from the cantonal office with the start date of the vocational school (usually one or two weeks after the start of the internship). Enrollment is automatic once the contract is registered. The student receives the class schedule, the school address, and the list of necessary school materials.
### Fiscal and pension management during the internship
During the internship, the apprentice accumulates contributions towards AHV (old-age and survivors' insurance), IV (disability insurance), and Maternity Insurance. These payments are mandatory and start from the first euro earned. [Pension management](nav:pension) is centralized: once the contract is registered, the company automatically contributes through the fund.
To navigate the tax system during the internship, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate the net monthly amount based on the gross salary and social contributions in Graubünden. If you have questions about annual tax management, consult the resources on the [tax return](nav:tax-return) to understand how the direct federal tax (DFT) works at the cantonal and municipal level. The declaration is mandatory if the income exceeds the cantonal threshold (not yet specified in the brief).

item.title: Reducing traffic: cheap tickets are not enough
item.description: An HSLU study reveals that convenience, secure parking and luggage transport are more important than price to encourage public transport.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - HSLU study: cheap tickets are not enough to reduce road traffic - 70% of trips and holidays take place by car; 92% for those who do not have a transport subscription - Convenience, parking and luggage matter more than the price - A change of means of transport reduces the choice of public transport by 31%
## Key facts - **What**: Study on leisure mobility and factors that encourage public transport - Where: Switzerland (HSLU Lucerne research, national spillovers) - Who: University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Lucerne (HSLU), Federal Office of Roads (USTRA), Widar von Arx (research manager) - Car share: 70% day trips and holidays; 92% among those who do not have a subscription - Critical factor: An additional change reduces the probability of public transport by 31% - Potential services: Door-to-door luggage transport would increase the use of public transport by 8 percentage points
The study by the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Lucerne (HSLU), commissioned by the Federal Office of Roads (USTRA), disassembles a commonplace widespread in Swiss mobility policy. Lowering ticket prices is not the main solution to convince Swiss people to give up their car during trips and holidays. The research, coordinated by Widar von Arx, identifies other much more relevant obstacles: practicality in travel, the certainty of finding a parking space at the destination and concrete services such as luggage transport.
The numbers of the study are explicit. In the ### The reality of Swiss public transport The study reveals a structural gap between the theoretical convenience of public transport and the practical choice of the car at the national level. It is not just a matter of economic sensitivity to price. Researchers observe that travelers are not very sensitive to ticket costs when on vacation. The value of free time and convenience prevail over the economic lever. This has direct implications for the cost of living in Switzerland: cantonal administrations, which plan public investments in mobility, must reconsider strategies based solely on tariff reduction. The practical solutions proposed by the HSLU research are concrete and immediately implementable. For those who continue to use the car, the certainty of finding parking at the destination could make travelers more willing to change their departure time, thus distributing traffic throughout the day rather than concentrating it during peak hours. Advance booking of parking and Park and Ride facilities are already feasible in many Swiss cantons, but are not yet standardized at the national level. Some cantons have invested in online systems, others have not. ### What role for additional services? The research suggests specific interventions on the practical disadvantages of public transport. A door-to-door service for luggage transport could increase the share of public transport use in day trips by up to 8 percentage points. At the national level, this would result in a significant redistribution of traffic on the roads. Direct connections, high service frequency, and coordinated mobility solutions for the last leg of the journey (the so-called 'last mile') are also important. These interventions would be more decisive than ticket discounts in effectively reducing road traffic.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What changes in daily practice
The HSLU study does not present miracle recipes, but rather clear priorities for public decision-makers and transport managers. There is no single measure capable of deeply changing travel habits: this is the clear conclusion of the researchers. To ease traffic, it is necessary to address the concrete needs of travelers. Certainty in planning, simple connections, and convenience must prevail over the sole economic lever. The Swiss cantons are already taking the first steps. Some have introduced online booking systems for parking near train stations. Other administrations are expanding Park and Ride coverage. However, national harmonization remains limited. The HSLU research provides an empirical basis to justify public investments in these directions, independently of hypothetical fiscal policies on cars or fuels.
### How to plan a trip using public transport
If you intend to reduce the use of your car during your trips in Switzerland, some concrete steps emerge from the research:
1. **Check available connections.** Consult the [public transport](nav:transport) website to find direct routes or with few changes to your destination. An additional change significantly reduces the likelihood of choice.
2. Book the parking in advance. If you still prefer to drive to a station, many cantons offer online booking systems to avoid wasting time looking for parking and to better distribute traffic flows.
3. Evaluate the [total cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) of the trip, not just the ticket. Include fuel, tolls, parking, and vehicle wear. Often, public transport turns out to be more economical than it seems at first glance.
4. Take advantage of seasonal offers. Many Swiss operators offer discounted tickets for trips, especially in the low season.
The HSLU study also suggests that improving comfort during the trip—such as through luggage transport services or special compartments for bicycles—makes public transport more attractive. The research concludes that reducing national road traffic requires a comprehensive vision: investments in practicality, not marginal discounts on tickets.

item.title: Apprenticeship in the Canton of Graubünden: internship and maturity
item.description: Complete guide to apprenticeship in Graubünden: how to find an internship, salary with social security contributions, guaranteed minimum holidays and federal professional maturity.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Swiss apprenticeship combines school teaching and company practice, regulated by AFC (federal) and cantons - Maximum hours 45-50 per week, minimum holidays 4 weeks (5 if underage) - Apprentice pays AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3%, no federal minimum wage - Professional maturity can be achieved in parallel or after, with national recognition
## Key facts - **What**: Dual vocational training system (company + vocational school) - Who regulates: AFC (Federal Office for Vocational Education and Training), cantonal administrations, municipalities - Duration: 2-4 years according to the vocational training order - Maximum hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices, sales), 50 hours (other sectors) - Pension contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee (total 10.6% with employer) - Minimum holidays: 4 weeks per year (5 for under 20) - Minimum wage: None federal, set by canton/sector/company
### The federal and cantonal system The apprenticeship in Switzerland is a vocational training path that combines school teaching and work practice in a company. It is regulated at the federal level by the Federal Office for Vocational Education and Training (AFC) and the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), and at the cantonal level by the competent local administrations. In the Canton of Grisons, as in all cantons, the competence for vocational training remains in the hands of the cantonal administration, which authorizes the training companies and registers the apprentices with the vocational schools.
Each canton follows common national principles to ensure the federal recognition of diplomas and the mobility of workers throughout Switzerland. The general structure provides for a training contract between the apprentice, the training company, and the vocational school, typically lasting between 2 and 4 years.
### Rights and obligations during the apprenticeship During the apprenticeship, the apprentice is entitled to protections guaranteed by federal labor laws: - Maximum hours: 45 hours per week (industry, offices, commerce) or 50 hours (agriculture, tourism, and other sectors) - Minimum holidays: 4 weeks per year (5 weeks if underage at the start of the apprenticeship) - Progressive remuneration: Usually increases every year; amounts set by collective labor agreements or company agreements - Protection from violation: Any agreement with hours or holidays below the legal minimum is null and void
### Apprentice social security As an employee, the apprentice must pay social security contributions. AVS/AI/IPG (old-age, disability, loss of earnings compensation) amount to 5.3% of gross salary; the employer pays the total 10.6%. Unemployment insurance (AD) and accidents (AC) correspond to 1.1% up to an annual maximum. Health insurance and accidents (LAINF) range from 0.7–1.5% depending on the sector.
These contributions are mandatory and ensure pension coverage in the Swiss system. There is no federal minimum wage for apprentices; the salary level is determined by the canton of residence, the professional sector, and the training company. Consult the vocational training office of the Canton of Grisons for specific amounts practiced in the region.
### Vocational school and federal orders The theoretical training takes place at cantonal vocational schools, usually 1-2 days a week or in intensive blocks. The programs follow federal initial vocational training orders (OPI), which set skills, content, and national standards recognized. The school covers both professional subjects and general culture (languages, mathematics, history, law). Enrollment in the school occurs automatically after registering the training contract with the cantonal authorities. ### The apprenticeship contract: essential elements
The apprenticeship contract is a legal document that regulates the relationship between the apprentice, the company, and the cantonal administration. It must contain specific information: the total duration of the apprenticeship (e.g., 3 years), the tasks and skills to be acquired, the monthly salary (gross salary), working days and holidays, the probationary period (usually 1-3 months), and early termination clauses. Both parties — the apprentice (or parent/guardian if a minor) and the company — must sign the contract in the presence of a notary or at the competent cantonal authority.
The apprentice's salary varies considerably depending on the sector (construction, healthcare, commerce, craftsmanship), the canton, and the company. Since there is no federal minimum wage for apprentices in Switzerland, the canton of residence plays a crucial role: some cantons have set regional minimum wages, while others leave it to negotiation. It is advisable to check with the cantonal office for vocational training in Graubünden for reference values and applicable collective labor agreements in your sector.
During the contract, the apprentice can benefit from protection against night work (federal laws prohibit night work for apprentices under 16, except in certain cases), and in some cantons, from financial subsidies in case of financial difficulties.
### Professional maturity: advancement path
After the apprenticeship (or in parallel during the last 1-2 years), the apprentice can obtain professional maturity, an additional federal diploma that allows direct access to universities of applied sciences (UAS) without an entrance exam. Professional maturity is recognized throughout Switzerland and is particularly valuable for those who wish to continue their studies after the apprenticeship or change their professional sector.
Professional maturity is obtained by passing exams in three areas: languages and communication (German and a foreign language), mathematics and sciences (mathematics, natural sciences), and professional disciplines (specific subjects of the chosen branch). The exams typically take place in the last months of the apprenticeship or immediately afterward. Federal recognition allows the diploma holder to enroll in any Swiss university of applied sciences, regardless of the canton where the diploma was obtained.
### Economic and tax considerations
During the apprenticeship, the gross salary declared is subject to mandatory deductions (AVS/AI/IPG, AD, AC, LAINF) that significantly reduce the net salary. The apprentice is required to subscribe to health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of the start of the apprenticeship; premiums vary by canton and region. The canton of Graubünden usually offers subsidies to reduce the premium in case of low income. It is important to plan the monthly budget considering these fixed costs and to check the available cantonal benefits.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Practical procedure: how to find an internship position
The first step is to consult the official portals that list available internship positions in the Canton of Graubünden and throughout Switzerland. The federal portal ASLAP (Federal Office for Vocational Education and Training) allows you to view offers filtered by canton and professional sector. The website of the Office for Vocational Education and Training of the Canton of Graubünden lists recognized training companies, addresses, contacts, and available training programs in the region. [nav:jobs] allows you to search for internship positions nationwide, along with platforms such as jobs.ch, indeed, and jobscout24. It is also useful to visit companies directly interested in your preferred sector and ask if they are looking for apprentices.
### Application and selection
Once you have identified the target companies, prepare a professional dossier: curriculum vitae (with school experiences, internships, extracurricular activities, language skills), cover letter (explain why you want this internship and this company), school certificates (compulsory school diploma and last year's report cards), and optional references from teachers or previous employers.
Apply through the channels indicated by the company (mail, email, online form). If the application is selected, a motivational interview will follow (the company verifies motivation and suitability for the role), possible aptitude tests (some companies require tests on mathematical, linguistic, and manual skills), and a visit to the company to get to know the workplace and the team.
### Signing the contract and cantonal registration
If selected, the company proposes a preliminary internship contract. The document must be read carefully and agreed upon every point: duration, remuneration, hours, holidays, probationary period. The apprentice (or parent/guardian if minor) and the company sign the contract in the presence of a cantonal official or notary. The Office for Vocational Education and Training of Graubünden registers the internship in the federal system and automatically enrolls the apprentice in the relevant vocational school. You will receive a summons for school, a lesson calendar, and a list of necessary materials.
### Timeline and deadlines
For an internship start in September (beginning of the Swiss school year): start looking for positions from October-November of the previous year, send applications from November to February, attend interviews and tests from February to April, sign the contract from April to June, cantonal registration from June to July, receive documentation in August, and start the internship in September. Some sectors have different schedules; check with the cantonal office for vocational education and training of Graubünden.
### Resources and next steps
For detailed information on the Swiss apprenticeship system and opportunities in the Canton of Graubünden, the AFC (www.sbfi.admin.ch) provides federal regulations, diploma recognitions, and contacts for cantonal offices. The Office for Vocational Education and Training of the Canton of Graubünden is available for addresses, hours, forms, and a list of training companies. Consult our [nav:calculator] to simulate gross and net salary considering the mandatory social security contributions (AVS/AI/IPG, AD, AC, LAINF). Visit [nav:jobs] to search for internship ads nationwide in your preferred sector.

item.title: Lease Freiburg: Tenant's Right Guide
item.description: Maximum deposit 3 months rent, cancellation on cantonal form, dispute within 30 days. The federal rules of the Bonds Code guarantee uniform protection in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Maximum security deposit of 3 months' rent (CO art. 253) - Landlord's notice valid only on official cantonal form - Objection within 30 days to the conciliation authority - Same rules throughout Switzerland, federal law
## Key facts - **What**: Federal tenancy law governed by the Code of Obligations - Where: Canton of Fribourg and all of Switzerland (identical rules) - Who: Tenants, landlords, cantonal conciliation authority - Amount: Maximum security deposit of 3 months' rent - Procedure: Notice on cantonal form; objection within 30 days - Protection: Blocked account in the tenant's name for the deposit
Swiss tenancy law is one of the most protected and uniform areas of law in the country: thanks to the Code of Obligations, which regulates the matter at the federal level, the rules are identical in every canton, including Fribourg. This means that a tenant in Fribourg enjoys the same legal protections as a tenant in Zurich, Geneva, or Valais. National uniformity eliminates ambiguities and ensures legal certainty for both tenants and landlords.
The security deposit is the first element that characterizes tenant protection. In the Canton of Fribourg, as in all of Switzerland, the deposit may not exceed three months' rent. If you rent an apartment for CHF 1,500 per month, the maximum deposit will be CHF 4,500. This limit is fixed and non-negotiable: the Code of Obligations expressly prohibits higher amounts.
A crucial aspect: the deposit must be paid into a blocked account in the tenant's name. This means that the money remains the tenant's property, and the landlord cannot use it for other purposes (e.g., to cover missing rents during the tenancy). The blocked account is a bilateral protection: it protects the tenant by ensuring that the deposit is not squandered, and it protects the landlord because the money remains available in case of damage.
### Notice and cantonal form
Notice is the formal communication with which one of the parties decides to terminate the contract. In the Canton of Fribourg, the landlord's notice is valid ONLY if made on an official form provided by the canton. Verbal communications, generic emails, or letters on private letterhead are not sufficient. This formal obligation responds to a fundamental principle of Swiss law: the certainty of form protects both parties by avoiding disputes over the validity of the communication.
The notice periods vary depending on the contract's seniority. During the first year, the notice period is 1 month. From the second to the ninth year, the notice period increases to 2 months. From the tenth year onwards, the notice period is 3 months. These terms protect the tenant by preventing sudden termination and ensuring sufficient time to find new accommodation.
One more clarification: although federal law establishes these terms for the landlord, the tenant must also respect the same deadlines when deciding to terminate the contract. The practical difference is that the tenant, while having to notify the notice in writing, is not strictly required to use the cantonal form (although it is recommended for clarity). The landlord, on the other hand, is obliged to use the official form. ### Dispute of initial fee and conciliation authority
If a tenant considers that the rent (the rent) proposed by the landlord is excessive with respect to the local market or the conditions of the property, he has the constitutional right to challenge it. This dispute must be submitted to the leasing conciliation authority of the Canton of Fribourg within 30 days of receipt of the rent notice.
The 30-day deadline is strict: a dispute filed on the 31st day will be inadmissible. For this reason it is essential to note the date of receipt of the communication of the rent (for example, the letter from the landlord) and mark the calendar with the deadline.
The conciliation authority does not evaluate the fee based on subjective criteria: it uses clear federal parameters. Article 269 of the Bond Code states that the "corrected initial fee" must meet the criteria of: - Location and location of the property - Construction and furnishing conditions - Services provided (heating, hot water, common services) - Fees for comparable properties in the same area
If the dispute is well-founded, the conciliation authority may order a reduction in the fee. If it is unfounded, the dispute is rejected and the proposed fee becomes binding.
# ## Other disputes that can be resolved by conciliation
The conciliation authority does not only resolve disputes over the initial fee.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Step-by-step procedure to challenge an excessive rent
If you are looking for a house in the Canton of Fribourg and the landlord proposes a rent that seems excessive to you, here is how to proceed:
**Step 1: Gather documentation** Note the exact date of receipt of the rent communication (letter, email with read receipt, or documented verbal communication). Keep all written communications from the landlord. Research the rents charged for similar properties in the area (use real estate listing sites, cantonal statistics, consultations with agents).
Step 2: Identify the cantonal conciliation authority In the Canton of Fribourg, the conciliation authority for rental matters is a specific cantonal office. Access the official website of the canton (www.fr.ch) and search for "conciliation authority" or "commission de conciliation immobilière". Note the address, email, and phone numbers.
Step 3: Prepare the written objection The objection must be submitted in writing (letter or form, if available). Clearly indicate: name and address of the property, rent proposed by the landlord, reason for the objection (e.g., "The rent is excessive compared to comparable properties in the area"), any evidence or market comparisons. Attach photos of the documentation or comparison ads.
Step 4: Send the objection within 30 days Send the objection by registered mail (with return receipt) to the conciliation authority. Ensure it arrives BEFORE the 30-day deadline. Keep the postal receipt as proof.
Step 5: Await summons The authority will examine the application and summon both parties (tenant and landlord) to a conciliation meeting. The meeting usually takes place at the authority's office.
Step 6: Attend the conciliation Present your arguments orally. Bring documents and photos. Listen to the landlord's counterarguments. The authority will mediate and, if possible, seek a compromise.
Step 7: Final report If an agreement is reached, the authority will draw up a report binding on both parties. If no agreement is reached, the authority will issue a decision (check, but generally the procedure is mediated, not decisional). If you are dissatisfied with the result, you have the right to appeal to the civil courts.
### Additional protections: the blocked account
Before paying the security deposit, ensure that the landlord deposits it in a blocked account (gebundenes Konto / compte bloqué) in your name. Request the bank documentation that proves the blocking. Some landlords try to keep it in a personal account: this is prohibited by law. If you notice this irregularity, you can immediately challenge it with the conciliation authority.
### Practical resources and contacts
To access forms, updated information on average rents in your canton, and calculation tools, consult our [cost of living calculator](nav:cost-of-living). It will help you understand how the rent fits into your overall budget and plan your finances before signing a contract.
Contact the conciliation authority of the Canton of Fribourg directly to receive the official objection form and clarifications on the procedure. Remember: rental law is federal and identical throughout Switzerland, but cantonal authorities have specific locations, hours, and administrative procedures.
