item.title: Permit B Valais: requirements and renewal
item.description: How to renew the residence permit B in Valais: the requirements, the necessary documents and the procedures at the Cantonal Office of Migration.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Permit B is a renewable long-term residence permit for foreigners - Valais has specific cantonal requirements and procedures - Renewal must be requested before expiration from the competent office - Required documents vary depending on the work situation
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit B for regular foreign residents - Where: Canton of Valais (Cantonal Migration Office) - Who: Foreigners living and working in Switzerland - Duration: Renewable periodically according to federal provisions - Federal authority: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) - Nature: Federal administrative authorization managed by the cantons
The residence permit B represents a form of authorization for foreign residents who wish to settle in Switzerland for an extended period. Unlike the permit L, valid for a short duration of up to one year, the permit B allows for long-term residence and is renewable according to the conditions set by federal and cantonal authorities. In the Canton of Valais, as in all Swiss cantons, the management of this administrative procedure is entrusted to the Cantonal Migration Office, which applies the federal principles established by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) and adapts them to local regulations.
### Difference between permits L, B, and C
Switzerland manages three main categories of permits for foreigners. The permit L is intended for short stays, up to one year, and is typically granted for fixed-term employment contracts or extended visits. The permit B is the form of authorization for those who intend to reside permanently in Switzerland for an intermediate period; it is renewable and represents the most common permit for foreign workers settling in the country. The permit C, finally, is the residence permit, normally granted after a prolonged period of residence (usually 10 years, or 5 years for citizens of the EU or EFTA) and provides a more stable and durable form of authorization.
### Who is entitled to permit B in Valais
To obtain a residence permit B in the Canton of Valais, the foreigner must meet a series of conditions established by federal regulations and cantonal directives. First, it is necessary to have a regular and declared occupation, or sufficient means of subsistence certified. A second fundamental requirement concerns housing: the applicant must have suitable housing in Switzerland, in compliance with local health and safety regulations. Furthermore, there must be no concrete danger to public security, public order, or other fundamental needs of the State; this means that the applicant must not have significant criminal records or have seriously violated Swiss legislation. Finally, the permit B is granted only to those who commit to respecting Swiss legislation in all its forms, both federal and cantonal and municipal. ### Fundamental Requirements for Permit B in Valais
The procedure for granting the residence permit B in Valais is based on several fundamental pillars verified by the cantonal authorities. The first is regular employment: the applicant must have a valid employment contract recognized by Swiss law. If the work is self-employed, it must be registered with the competent commercial authorities. A second requirement is the availability of suitable housing: the Cantonal Migration Office verifies that the accommodation meets Swiss standards of health, square footage, and compliance with building and health protection regulations. A third element concerns the financial situation: the applicant must not represent an economic burden on the Swiss social security system, so they must prove sufficient financial means. Finally, public order conditions must be met: no ongoing criminal proceedings, no convictions for serious crimes, and no expulsion orders in force.
### Documents to be Produced for Renewal
To renew the residence permit B in Valais, the applicant must complete an official form provided by the Cantonal Migration Office and attach a series of supporting documents. The applicant's valid passport or identity document is mandatory; it must have sufficient validity to cover the requested authorization period. The current [employment contract](nav:jobs), signed by the employer, is essential to prove regular employment; it must include identifying data, job duties, duration, compensation, and place of work. An up-to-date criminal record certificate, issued by the competent authorities of the country of origin or previous residence, is required to attest to the absence of relevant criminal convictions. Proof of housing, which can consist of a lease agreement, a statement from the owner, or a receipt for housing expenses, is necessary to demonstrate the availability of suitable accommodation. If the applicant is resident in Valais and has a family, updated civil status certificates, school certificates for minor children, or documentation relating to dependents may be required. [Tax and bank certificates](nav:banks) attesting to the applicant's financial solvency may be requested by the authorities.
### Renewal Procedure and Deadlines
The renewal of the residence permit B in Valais must be initiated before the expiration of the current authorization. The cantonal authorities advise submitting the renewal application at least three months before the permit's expiration date to ensure the application is processed without interruption in legal residence. The renewal application must be submitted directly to the Valais Cantonal Migration Office. Some cantons allow online submission via a portal, while others require paper submission at counters; Valais will follow its specific administrative procedures. Once the application is submitted, the Office will review the presented documents, verify the persistence of the requirements, and, if necessary, contact the applicant to request additional information or clarifications. Processing times typically range from four to eight weeks but may be extended in case of in-depth verifications.

item.description: Guide to compulsory sick pay premiums in the canton of Valais: deductibles available, insurance models, premium reduction and procedure for obtaining cantonal subsidies.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - LAMal is mandatory in Valais with premiums varying by age and insurance model - Available deductibles: from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 for adults - Premium reduction is a cantonal subsidy for low- to middle-income families - Deadline for changing health insurance: December 31 of the previous year
## Key facts - **What**: Mandatory health insurance (LAMal) with per capita premiums and variable deductibles - Where: Canton of Valais; mandatory for residents domiciled in the canton - Who: All residents; mandatory within 3 months of arrival - When: Annual premiums; change of insurance company by December 31 for effect from January 1 - Models: Basic insurance, HMO, network, models with high deductible - Deductibles: CHF 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, 2,500 for adults - Subsidies: Premium reduction managed by the canton of Valais for income and asset brackets
In the canton of Valais, as in the rest of Switzerland, the mandatory health insurance (LAMal) covers residents and foreigners domiciled in any canton. Premiums are managed at the cantonal-regional level and vary based on age brackets, chosen insurance models, and deductibles. Valais, like every canton, has a premium reduction system (cantonal subsidy) aimed at families that do not reach certain income levels.
The system's structure is private: health insurance companies operate with per capita premiums (i.e., calculated for each individual), NOT as a salary contribution or tax. This means that each family member pays their own premium, regardless of age or economic condition — except for cantonal subsidies for low incomes.
### Premium brackets and deductibles in Valais
In the canton of Valais, several health insurance companies operate. Premiums are communicated annually by individual insurers and registered at the cantonal level. For adults, the available deductibles are six: CHF 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, and 2,500. A higher deductible (e.g., 2,500) results in a lower monthly premium, as the insured accepts to cover a larger share of healthcare costs before the insurance kicks in.
Children benefit from separate deductibles, generally more favorable than those for adults. Mandatory LAMal includes basic coverage (essential services: hospital, outpatient medicine, drugs, maternity, accidents for those without separate accident insurance). On this basis, additional optional coverages (dentist, physiotherapy, alternative medicines) can be added — optional and NOT regulated by LAMal.
Keyword: the premium is PER CAPITA. If a family of four resides in Valais, they will pay four separate premiums (one for each member), even if they choose the same deductible and the same health insurance company.
[Compare health insurance companies and LAMal premiums for your profile](nav:health) The reduction of premiums (cantonal subsidy) is a crucial tool for families and self-employed workers with limited income. In the canton of Valais, as in almost all cantons, the responsible cantonal authority evaluates the total income of the household (cantonal taxable income, possibly adjusted) and the assets, and grants a monthly contribution that directly reduces the LAMal premium due.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Procedure to obtain the premium reduction
Those living in the canton of Valais and with a low to medium income should consult the cantonal office responsible for social services or health. In Valais, the competent authority is indicated on the official cantonal portal (www.vs.ch) or at the municipality of residence.
Step-by-step of the request:
1. **Gather documentation**: [cantonal tax return](nav:tax-return) for the last two years (extract of taxable income and taxed assets), pay slip or certificate of self-employed income, certificate of family composition from the municipality.
2. Check income limits: contact the competent cantonal office and obtain the exact access criteria for the current year (a couple without children with a joint taxable income up to CHF 80,000–100,000 can generally access the reduction, depending on local parameters).
3. Submit application: fill out the reduction request form (usually available online on the Valais portal or at the municipal office) and send it by post or in digital format.
4. Decision and payment: the office evaluates the request within about 4–6 weeks and communicates the monthly subsidy amount. The contribution is paid directly to the selected insurer, reducing the premium due.
5. Annual renewal: the reduction is granted for the calendar year; by December 31, it is necessary to renew the request if the income conditions remain unchanged.
### Deadlines and change of health insurance
The deadline to change health insurance is December 31 of each year, effective from January 1 of the following year. The notice of termination from the old insurer must be received by the insurer by that date, preferably by registered mail or through the online portal. If the reduction is approved, it is advisable to communicate the grant number or the estimated contribution to the new health insurance to avoid incorrect billing.
Those who do not change insurers by December 31 automatically renew the annual contract on the same policy; in this case, the premium is fixed until December 31 of the following year (premium changes are valid only at the contract expiration).
Practical advice: check the premium list of available insurers in Valais at least three months before the deadline, both for the basic model and for alternatives (HMO, network), to evaluate which combination (insurer + deductible + model + estimated reduction) offers the lowest total annual cost.

item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The B permit is a renewable residence permit for foreigners in Switzerland - The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) regulates the criteria at the federal level - Renewal: the concrete procedures are managed by the Fribourg cantonal administration - Documents and requirements vary for EU/EFTA citizens and third countries
## Key facts - **What**: B residence permit — renewable residence and work permit - Who: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) — federal authority - Where: Canton of Fribourg — cantonal migration administration - Duration: Renewable according to federal and cantonal decisions - Category: EU/EFTA foreigners and third countries
The B permit is the most common residence permit for those living and working in Switzerland, including the Canton of Fribourg. Unlike the L permit (short duration up to one year), the B permit is renewable and allows for a more stable stay in the Swiss territory. The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), a federal body, establishes the general criteria and competencies; however, the concrete procedures for application and renewal remain with the Fribourg cantonal administration.
### Who can apply for the B permit in Fribourg The legal status varies between citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association (EU/EFTA) and foreigners from third countries. Both categories can access the B permit, but with sometimes different requirements and documentation. The main difference concerns access to the labor market and the conditions of stay in the territory: those with EU/EFTA status benefit from more favorable conditions compared to third countries.
General requirements include: having a confirmed job offer or a stable employment situation, demonstrating self-financing capacity, possessing [mandatory health insurance](nav:health), and complying with the stay conditions defined by the federal and cantonal authorities. The lack of one of these elements can result in the rejection of the application or a referral for clarification.
### The role of the Fribourg administration The Fribourg cantonal migration office manages practically all instances of application, renewal, and modification of the B permit. Although the fundamental regulations are issued by the SEM at the federal level, it is the cantonal administration that evaluates individual files, requests additional documentation, and issues the permit. For those residing or intending to move to Fribourg for work reasons, it is advisable to contact the Fribourg cantonal administration directly to know the updated forms, specific deadlines, and methods of submitting the file. ## Renewal of the B permit: procedures and timelines
Unlike other permit categories, the B permit is not unlimited: it has a fixed duration set by federal and cantonal authorities at the time of initial issuance. When this duration is about to expire, it is necessary to request a renewal from the competent cantonal administration, in this case, the offices of Fribourg. The renewal procedure generally follows the same guidelines as the initial application: it is necessary to demonstrate that the original conditions persist (employment, self-financing, [health insurance](nav:health)). However, the administrative process is sometimes more streamlined, as the authorities already have historical information about the applicant.
### How to obtain information on deadlines and procedures
The first step is to contact the cantonal administration of Fribourg directly. Online, it is possible to find: official forms for renewal, list of required documents (identity card, employment contract, health insurance certificate, criminal record extracts if necessary), cantonal and municipal administrative costs, and indicative processing times. This information is essential for planning the procedure in advance.
### Implications for those working and residing in Fribourg
For those who already hold a B permit and reside permanently in Fribourg for work reasons, renewal is a crucial aspect of medium-term planning. [Self-financing and cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) are factors that the administration evaluates carefully. A lack of timely renewal can lead to the loss of legal residence status and, consequently, to occupational and tax complications. It is therefore essential to schedule the expiration date and start the renewal procedure at least 2-3 months before the deadline to avoid bureaucratic delays.
### Third-country nationals vs. EU/EFTA citizens
An important practical difference concerns the times and documentation: EU/EFTA citizens generally benefit from faster administrative processes and less stringent documentation requirements. Third-country nationals may face longer duration assessments and additional clarification requests. The SEM provides general guidelines at the federal level; however, each canton (including Fribourg) applies small procedural variants. Consulting local authorities directly remains the most reliable strategy to comply with all prescriptions.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## Practical checklist: how to proceed with the renewal
Here are the concrete steps for those who need to renew their B permit in Fribourg:
**1. Identify the expiration date**: Check the expiration date written on the current B permit. This is the absolute starting point.
2. Contact the Fribourg administration: Find the phone number and address of the Fribourg cantonal migration office through the official website of the canton.
3. Request the updated forms: Ask which are the official forms for renewal and the exact checklist of required documents.
4. Gather the documents: Generally, a valid passport or ID card, current employment contract or letters from the company confirming employment, Swiss health insurance certificate, residence certificate (sometimes issued by the municipality), documentation of income level if relevant, and criminal record extract (mandatory in some cantons) are required.
5. Submit the complete dossier: Start the renewal procedure at least 2-3 months before the expiration date. Submit the complete dossier to avoid requests for additional information that prolong the process.
6. Monitor the status of the application: The administration will communicate the status of the application by mail or email. Respond promptly to any requests for clarification.
7. Pick up the new permit: Once approved, the new B permit will be available for pickup at the cantonal office.
### Tools for planning self-financing
If you are a resident in Switzerland and want to calculate your tax obligations or better understand your net salary (a crucial element to demonstrate self-financing during renewal), you can use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator). This tool helps plan the economic management of your stay in Switzerland and document the income level required by the administration.
### When to contact a specialized consultant
If your personal situation is complex (imminent change of employer, previous permits with particular histories, family situations with dependents), it is advisable to consult a Swiss immigration law expert before submitting the renewal. A consultant can verify that your documentation is complete and that there are no procedural obstacles.
Keep your documents always up-to-date and monitor the permit deadlines with precision. To receive monthly information on permits, taxation, and job opportunities in Switzerland, [access the Frontaliere Ticino calculator](nav:calculator).

item.title: Nursery: gaps in controls on minors
item.description: An educator reported for child pornography worked in a kindergarten for two years. How and why institutional controls failed in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - A kindergarten educator reported in 2024 for pedopornographic interests - Continued to work undisturbed until arrest in July 2026 - Criminal record remained clean, no ban on contact with minors
## Key facts - **What**: Report of online pedopornographic interests not followed by preventive actions - When: January 2024 (report); June 2026 (critical episode); July 2026 (arrest) - Where: Kindergarten in Saint-Sulpice (Canton Vaud) - Who: An educator, Federal Police, Public Prosecutor's Office of North Vaud, parents - Origin of report: National Center for Missing and Exploited Children - Initial outcome: No prosecution by the Public Prosecutor
In January 2024, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children reported to the Federal Police the online activities of a kindergarten educator in Saint-Sulpice (VD), which showed clear pedopornographic interests. The report was forwarded to the Public Prosecutor's Office of North Vaud, which however issued a no prosecution decision with a surprising justification: it was considered the "first complaint" and it was probably the case that the man "was not aware of acting illegally."
This decision had a critical consequence: the educator's criminal record remained clean. No criminal proceedings meant no ban on working with minors. And so, for two years, the man continued to operate in the public kindergarten without any restrictions.
### The first alarm from parents
At one point, the three-year-old son of a couple reported that an adult at the kindergarten had given him "kisses on the mouth and strokes on the head." The mother contacted the management of the facility, asking for reassurances about the professional profiles of the staff. According to the account in the newspaper 24heures, the management "seemed to doubt the child's words," even though they received the parents in repeated meetings over the following months. The parents emphasized that the child had never spoken negatively about the other educators, with whom he had a very good relationship; his reports always concerned the same man.
The most serious element emerged in June 2026: the child reported that the same man had touched his penis and shown him his own. At that point, investigators acted and the educator was arrested in July 2026. It was only during the subsequent investigations that the 2024 report to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children emerged — a report that no one at the facility, the Municipality, or the Canton knew about.
### The void in coordination between institutions
What emerges from the case is an alarming picture of absent coordination between the Federal Police, the Cantonal Public Prosecutor's Office, the Canton of Vaud, and the Municipality of Saint-Sulpice. The Public Prosecutor's Office argued that, since no criminal proceedings had been opened (due to the no prosecution decision), it could not impose a ban on participating in activities involving contact with minors.
The Municipality of Saint-Sulpice stated to the newspaper that they knew nothing about it, adding that "they had received the green light from the Canton, which is responsible for checking criminal records." But the Canton, in turn, had not received any communication about the 2024 report. The report from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children had remained confined within the Federal Police → Public Prosecutor's Office circuit, without feeding any information flow towards the Canton or towards the subjects who should have carried out prevention and control. ### The Fragmented Chain of Responsibility
In Switzerland, the control of criminal records for operators of childcare facilities is a grey area shared between several institutional levels. The Federal Police manages coordination with international bodies such as the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. The Public Prosecutor's Office of the cantons is responsible for deciding whether to initiate criminal proceedings. The Cantons administer the authorities that grant permits to childcare facilities and formally check the records at the time of recruitment. Municipalities directly manage public kindergartens.
In the case of Saint-Sulpice, each of these entities acted within its scope, without the information passing laterally. This is not an isolated case: the Swiss system of child protection is based on compartmentalization between federal, cantonal and municipal competences, without robust mechanisms for sharing reports external to official criminal proceedings.
### ### Failure in horizontal communication
The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children report came to the Federal Police in January 2024. The Public Prosecutor's Office has notified the Public Prosecutor's Office of northern Vodese. But that's where it all stopped. The Public Prosecutor's Office, deciding not to proceed, did not communicate the fact to either the Canton or the Municipality of Saint-Sulpice.

About sixty parliamentarians, following the case of Saint-Sulpice and others like it, asked Bern to create a blacklist (or more properly, a centralized list of reports) of childcare facility operators reported for inappropriate behavior. Such a list would allow you to: - Cantons and municipalities to check with an official instrument if a candidate has been reported in the past (even without conviction) - Cantonal authorities to obtain information beyond the borders of the official criminal record - International institutions to record risk signals even when they do not follow concluded criminal proceedings - Facilities to make a more conscious assessment at the time of hiring

item.title: Zug inheritance tax: rates and exemptions
item.description: In the Canton of Zug, inheritance and gift taxes are cantonal matters. Spouse and descendant exemptions, kinship rates: how the declaration works.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Inheritance tax is a cantonal, not federal, matter in Switzerland - Spouses and direct descendants benefit from exemptions or reduced rates - Mandatory declaration within deadlines set by the canton - Each canton sets its own rates, updated periodically
## Key facts - **What**: Inheritance and gift tax - Where: Canton of Zug and all of Switzerland - Who: Heirs, beneficiaries of gifts, donors - Exemptions: Spouse, children, descendants according to cantonal legislation - Scope: Matter of cantonal law, decentralized tax management
In Switzerland, the taxation of inheritances and gifts is the exclusive responsibility of the Cantons. The Canton of Zug, like all other Swiss cantons, has enacted its own cantonal legislation that regulates the rates, exemptions, and declaration procedures for inheritances and gifts. Unlike many European countries, the Federal Council does not set uniform rates at the national level: each canton decides autonomously how and how much to tax the transfer of wealth between generations.
This federalist structure creates a variety of tax scenarios depending on the domicile of the deceased or the donor at the time of death or donation. For those residing in Zug, it is crucial to understand the specific regime of the canton, particularly the rates applied for degree of kinship (spouse, descendants, collaterals, strangers) and any possible exemptions or franchises.
### Why inheritance remains a cantonal matter
Inheritance and gift taxes constitute an important item in cantonal tax revenues, although less than income and property taxes. Their structure reflects principles of tax equity and family protection: in almost all cantons, the spouse and direct children benefit from total exemptions or significantly reduced rates. The federal direct tax, by comparison, affects the annual income of every Swiss resident according to the federal rate added to the cantonal multipliers. Inheritance taxes, on the other hand, are applied once at the time of wealth transfer and vary deeply from one canton to another. ### Exemptions and rates by degree of kinship
In the Swiss cantonal system, the degree of kinship is the first element that determines the amount of tax due. The cantonal legislator protects the close family with total or very favorable exemptions. In many cantons, the widowed spouse is completely exempt from inheritance tax on the assets inherited from the deceased spouse. Similarly, direct children (and their descendants, if the child has died) enjoy total exemptions or very low rates—often halved or even lower than those for non-direct relatives.
For more distant relatives (brothers, sisters, uncles, cousins), the rate increases progressively. For strangers (people with no kinship to the deceased), the rate is even higher. Furthermore, many cantons, including Zug, apply a tiered system based on the amount of the inheritance: exemptions are often provided for small amounts, and the rate increases for brackets of movable and immovable wealth.
### Gifts between living individuals
As for gifts, the treatment is sometimes more favorable than for inheritances (because the donor is still alive and can benefit from personal income tax deductions), or it is equated to the inheritance treatment. Here too, the spouse and children often receive exemptions or significant reductions. In Zug, as in other cantons, gifts are subject to declaration with the Cantonal Administration of Finance.
### Declaration procedure and deadlines
The inheritance declaration is a mandatory obligation: the heirs or the administrators of the estate must communicate to the cantonal tax office (in the case of Zug, the Cantonal Administration of Finance) the composition of the deceased's estate within the deadlines set by cantonal law. The deadlines vary from canton to canton, generally from three months to one year from the death.
During this phase, it is necessary to provide a detailed inventory of the assets (money, securities, real estate, valuable movable property) and debts of the deceased. The tax office applies the rates in force at the time of the declaration and notifies the taxation by means of a tax notice. The heir must pay the tax within the deadline indicated in the notice, otherwise late interest and possible administrative penalties will be applied.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Step-by-step procedure to declare the inheritance in Zug
If you are an heir or administrator of an inheritance in the Canton of Zug, the procedure to follow is structured in five essential steps:
1. Verify the declaration deadline. Check with the Canton of Zug's Financial Administration the deadline by which to submit the inheritance declaration. Generally, the deadline starts from the day of death. Failure to comply with the deadline results in penalties and interest.
**2. Gather complete documentation.** Collect the death certificate, the will (if any), the list of the deceased's assets, bank documents, stock certificates, real estate documents, life insurance policies, and any proof of debts or encumbrances on the assets.
3. Fill out the official declaration form. Use the form provided by the Zug cantonal tax office. The form includes separate sections for real estate, credits, liquid assets in current account or cash, securities, life insurance, valuable movable assets, debts, and burdens.
4. Submit the declaration within the deadline. Deliver the completed and signed declaration to the Canton of Zug's Financial Administration, preferably in person or by registered mail to have proof of receipt and official tracking.
5. Receive and verify the tax assessment notice. After administrative verification, the canton will issue a notice communicating the amount of tax due. Verify that the applied rates correspond to your degree of kinship and the exemptions and brackets provided by the current cantonal law.
### Where to find the specific rates of Zug
Since each canton periodically updates its rates (sometimes every year with adjustments), it is essential to consult directly with the Canton of Zug's Financial Administration to obtain the current rates for each degree of kinship, mobile and immobile wealth bracket, and any exemptions. You can find this information on the official website of the Canton of Zug or by contacting the competent office directly.
Furthermore, if the inheritance includes real estate in more than one canton (e.g., a property in Zug and one in Ticino), each canton will apply its rates to the share of assets located in its territory. Consult the [tax return](nav:tax-return) to better understand the tax obligations in Switzerland and how to manage the tax situation after an inheritance.

item.title: Wages and the labour market in the canton of Zug: sectors and levels
item.description: Swiss labour market: how wage determination works between collective agreements, cantonal taxation and education levels.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - No federal minimum wage; some cantons provide it (including Canton Zugo) - Collective agreements determine wages for about 50% of Swiss workers - Federal + cantonal + municipal taxes reduce gross salary - Level of education (VET/maturity/degree) is a key factor in the salary scale
## Key facts - **What**: Wage determination (federal + cantonal + collective agreements) - Where: Each canton has its own laws (Canton Zugo included) - Who: Workers, unions, employers' associations, cantonal authorities - When: Biennial/triennial negotiations (contracts); annual taxation - Framework: FDF (federal) + cantonal + municipal (multiplier) - Hours: Max 45 hours/week (industry, offices, sales) or 50 hours (other sectors) - Holidays: Min 4 weeks (5 for those under 20) - Contributions: AHV/AI/IV 5.3%; AD/AC 1.1%; LAINF 0.7–1.5%
In Switzerland, there is no federal minimum wage. This is the first major difference compared to many other European countries: wage determination depends mainly on three factors — the federal regulatory framework, cantonal laws, and collective labor agreements. In Canton Zugo, as in every Swiss canton, this combination applies with its own local variables. Understanding how the Swiss labor market works is essential for anyone working or seeking employment in Switzerland.
The federal regulatory framework sets common minimum standards: maximum hours (45 hours per week for industry, offices, and sales; 50 hours for other sectors), minimum holidays (4 weeks, 5 for those under 20), maternity (14 weeks at 80% of salary with maternity allowance), paternity (2 weeks). These are the "pillars" that apply throughout Switzerland, from Canton Zugo to Ticino, from Valais to St. Gallen. But the real determinant of gross and net wages is the combination of collective agreements, local market dynamics, and cantonal tax regime.
### Collective agreements and wage determination
Collective labor agreements are negotiated between unions and employers' associations (or individual employers) that set minimum wages, working conditions, and benefits for entire sectors or professional categories. In Switzerland, about 50% of the dependent workforce is covered by collective agreements. When you receive a [pay slip](nav:payslip), you will see how your gross salary was calculated based on the collective agreement applied by your company.
A collective agreement can cover an entire sector (e.g., banking, insurance, hospitality, manufacturing) or a specific group of companies. Each contract specifies a minimum salary scale based on seniority, level of education, and professional role. For example, a collective agreement in the manufacturing sector might set a different minimum salary for someone with a VET (Vocational Education and Training) diploma compared to someone with a high school diploma or a university degree.
In Canton Zugo, as in other cantons, the main sectors (industry, finance, trade, services, healthcare) almost all have collective agreements in force. These agreements are renewed periodically (usually every 2-4 years) and reflect market dynamics, inflation, and economic conditions. When contracts are renegotiated, one of the main points of discussion between unions and employers is always the wage increase, with significant variations depending on the sector and economic period. If you work in a company that applies a collective agreement, you are covered by it even if you are not a union member (so-called "erga omnes effect" in many cantons).
For sectors where there is no collective agreement, remuneration is determined by individual negotiation and market conditions — the employer and the worker negotiate the salary and employment conditions directly.
## Cantonal taxation and impact on net salary
When an employer offers a gross salary, the worker does not receive the full amount declared. The difference between gross and net depends on two fundamental elements: social contributions (AVS/AI/IPG, unemployment insurance, accident insurance, possibly occupational insurance) and taxes (federal, cantonal and municipal).
In Switzerland, the tax system is structured on three levels: direct federal tax (DFI), cantonal taxes and municipal taxes. Each canton has its own municipal rates and multipliers — meaning that two workers with the same gross salary in different cantons will have significantly different net salaries. This applies to the Canton of Zug as well as to any other canton.
### Federal, cantonal and municipal taxation
The direct federal tax is uniform throughout Switzerland and follows the same progressive rates. However, the IFD is only the first level. In the Canton of Zug (as in every canton), the cantonal tax is added, which varies from canton to canton. To understand in detail how these rates work, see the [dichiarazione delle imposte](nav:tax-return) guide, which explains the federal and cantonal system. In addition, each municipality in the canton of Zug applies a multiplier to the cantonal tax, which further amplifies the variations between municipalities. A worker residing in Zurich (the capital, generally with lower multiplier)
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Where to find information about the job market in the Canton of Zug
Knowing how the Swiss job market works is the first step; knowing where to find concrete information is the second. If you work or are looking for a job in the Canton of Zug (or in any other canton), there are specific tools and resources to check the salaries in your sector, understand the current collective agreements, and calculate your net income.
The cantonal employment office of the Canton of Zug (Amt für Wirtschaft, Abteilung Arbeit) publishes data and statistics on the local job market. At the national level, the Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS) and SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) provide detailed surveys on median salaries by sector, level of education, and Swiss region. A very useful tool is the SECO Salary Portal, which allows you to compare average salaries by profession and region. If you are looking for a current collective agreement in your sector, contact the main union in your professional field or the relevant employers' association. Even if you are not unionized, the collective agreement often applies anyway: a company that applies a collective agreement must guarantee at least the minimum conditions provided by the agreement to all workers (including non-members).
### Calculate your net salary and negotiate consciously
Once you know the proposed gross salary (or your current salary), it is essential to understand how much you will take home net. The [salary calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to enter your annual gross income, your canton of residence, and your municipality, and it automatically calculates federal, cantonal, and municipal taxes, as well as social contributions. This tool is invaluable when you want to: evaluate a job offer (compare salaries in different cantons), plan your available income for your family budget, understand the impact of inflation and contract renewals on your actual paycheck.
When negotiating a salary, always do so based on official market data. If you know the average salary for your profession, experience, and level of education in your canton (thanks to UST/BFS data), you will have a solid starting point for your research and negotiations. In sectors with a collective agreement, there is often less room for individual negotiation — the salary is already set by the agreement — but for senior positions, specialized roles, or those without an applicable collective agreement, negotiation is the standard. Remember that the first year of employment is a critical period: in Switzerland, during the first year, the employer can terminate the contract with one month's notice, making post-hiring negotiation less effective than before signing.
Understanding the Swiss job market — from how collective agreements work to the cantonal tax variations — is crucial for making informed decisions about your career. Each canton has its own peculiarities, and the Canton of Zug, while one of the most economically dynamic in Switzerland, follows the same federal rules as any other canton. If you are looking for a job or want to evaluate an offer, start exploring the market in your sector with official data (UST, SECO, unions) and use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to see your realistic net income. Knowledge and transparency are your best allies in negotiating fair working conditions in any Swiss canton.

item.title: Half a billion to the farmers to save the agreement with Mercosur
item.description: The Foreign Policy Commission of the Council of States proposes 517 million francs for Swiss peasants.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - The Foreign Policy Committee of the Council of States proposes 517 million francs for Swiss farmers. - The free trade agreement with Mercosur is at risk after the rejection by the National Council. - The left threatens a referendum if deforestation and forced labor are not excluded.
## Key facts - **What**: Proposal of 517 million francs for Swiss farmers. - When: Discussion in autumn. - Where: Council of States. - Who: Foreign Policy Committee of the Council of States. - Amount: 517 million francs.
The Foreign Policy Committee of the Council of States is ready to make an important concession to Swiss farmers to save the free trade agreement with Mercosur countries. On Friday, it expressed its support for granting just over half a billion francs to Swiss producers. The agreement will now be discussed by the full chamber of the Council of States during the next session, following the rejection by the National Council last June. The left maintains the threat of a referendum.
In June, the farmers' lobby exerted its political weight to derail the agreement negotiated between the European Free Trade Association countries (Switzerland, Norway, Liechtenstein, and Iceland) and Mercosur at the National Council. An agreement born after 8 years of negotiations, seen as an important outlet for Swiss products on a market of 270 million people, but perceived as a danger by Swiss farmers and livestock breeders, who fear heavy losses due to the arrival of low-cost products with lower standards than those required of them.
### Implications for Swiss Agriculture
The proposal by the Foreign Policy Committee of the Council of States to grant 517 million francs to Swiss farmers represents an attempt to balance the concerns of the agricultural sector with the economic interests linked to the free trade agreement with Mercosur. This amount, although lower than the over 800 million francs requested by the agricultural world, is significantly higher than the 158 million francs provided by the Federal Council.
The issue goes beyond Mercosur; it is about supporting the concept of an economic policy based on free trade agreements to promote our exports. The Council of States will vote in the autumn session starting on September 14, and the proposal should gather the necessary votes to send a compromise to the National Council that would turn many "no" votes from the right into "yes" votes, leaving the left in the minority.
If the Amazon rainforest and forced labor are excluded from the agreement, the referendum remains on the table, as indicated by the Social Democratic Party councilor from Solothurn, Franziska Roth. Proposals to ban the import of goods produced, wholly or partly, with forced labor and to adopt the EU's deforestation regulations were both rejected, with 9 votes to 4 and 8 votes to 4 with 1 abstention, respectively.
The final word on the free trade agreement with Mercosur countries could then be up to the people. ## Practical Analysis
The free trade agreement with Mercosur represents a significant challenge for Swiss agriculture. Swiss farmers and livestock breeders fear that the arrival of low-cost products with lower standards could jeopardize their economic sustainability. The proposal of the Foreign Policy Committee of the Council of States to grant 517 million francs to Swiss producers is an attempt to mitigate these concerns.
### Comparison with the Previous Situation
Before the Committee's proposal, the Federal Council had planned only 158 million francs to support Swiss farmers. The new proposal represents a significant increase, although it does not reach the over 800 million francs requested by the agricultural world. This increase could help compensate for potential losses due to competition from imported products from Mercosur.
### Possible Scenarios
If the free trade agreement with Mercosur is approved with the conditions proposed by the Committee, Swiss farmers would receive significant financial support. ## In brief - Trial in Zurich for six members of 'Junge Tat' - Charges of discrimination and incitement to hatred - Prosecutor seeks prison sentences for main defendants
## Key facts - **What**: Trial for discrimination and incitement to hatred - When: Today - Where: Zurich - Who: Six members of 'Junge Tat' - Amount: Prison sentences requested
Today, six members of the far-right group 'Junge Tat' appeared before Zurich's justice system on charges of discrimination and incitement to hatred. During the hearing, the prosecutor requested prison sentences for the two main defendants, while the defense called for their acquittal. Outside the courthouse, about a hundred anti-fascist protesters gathered. The verdict will be pronounced only later.
This morning, the Public Prosecutor's Office requested a prison sentence of fifteen months, with six months to be served, against the two main defendants, Tobias Lingg (23) and Manuel Corchia (25). According to the prosecution, their actions exceeded the limits of freedom of expression. Both recidivists, they refused to answer the judge's questions.
In the afternoon, their defense lawyers instead asked for their clients to be acquitted of charges of discrimination, incitement to hatred, and violation of freedom of belief and worship. They invoked freedom of expression. According to Lingg's lawyer, the group's leader should only be sentenced to a conditional fine for minor offenses. For Corchia, complete acquittal was requested.
The first incriminating episode dates back to June 2022, when masked individuals attempted to disrupt a mass at the Church of Saints Peter and Paul during Pride, with the aim of placing a 2.4-meter-tall white wooden cross on a cement base with the inscription 'Nopridemonth' (literally no to a month of pride parade) inside the building. According to the prosecution, this way they disturbed the religious celebration, ridiculed the attendees, and caused damage to the stone floor of nearly 9,000 francs. The prosecution evaluates this action as discrimination based on sexual orientation and violation of freedom of worship and religion.
The second episode, which occurred in October of the same year, refers to a disturbance during a reading by drag queens intended for children at the Tanzhaus in Zurich. Three people who entered the building, where about fifty people were present, secretly recorded some conversations and attempted to unfurl a banner. Outside the building, other group members lit fireworks, chanted slogans, and distributed leaflets. According to the indictment, the smoke and threatening behavior frightened the attendees so much that, out of fear, they were unable to leave the building.
The court also dealt with several unauthorized actions carried out on the roofs of various buildings. In November 2022, some group members climbed onto the roof of the main building of the Basel train station, unfurled a banner reading 'Expel criminals,' and set off smoke bombs. They acted similarly in April 2024 in Winterthur (ZH), where they hung a banner dedicated to the theme of repatriation on a building. As early as May 2022, they climbed onto a crane in Zurich.
Today the courtroom was packed. In addition to numerous journalists, members of 'Junge Tat' were present, as well as organizers of events disrupted by the far-right group. Outside, about a hundred people gathered before the trial began to protest against right-wing extremism.
As mentioned, at the end of the hearing, the Zurich District Court had not yet decided on the manner and date of the verdict. ## Practical Implications
The trial in Zurich against members of 'Junge Tat' raises important questions regarding freedom of expression and discrimination in Switzerland. The prosecution requested prison sentences for the two main defendants, Tobias Lingg and Manuel Corchia, while the defense invoked their acquittal, arguing that their actions fall within freedom of expression.
The group's actions, such as interrupting a Pride Mass and disrupting a children's reading, caused material and psychological damage. The prosecution assessed these actions as discrimination based on sexual orientation and violation of freedom of worship and religion.
The case highlights the tension between freedom of expression and the need to protect the rights of minorities. The final ruling of the Zurich District Court will be crucial in establishing the limits of freedom of expression in Switzerland.

The court also examined several unauthorized actions taken on the roofs of various buildings. In November 2022, some members of the group had climbed onto the roof of the main building of the Basel train station, unfurled a banner with the words' Expel criminals' and lit smoke bombs. They had acted in a similar way in April 2024 in Winterthur (ZH), where a banner dedicated to the theme of repatriation had been hung on a building.

## In brief - Police intervention ended in Goldach after a school party - About 300 people evacuated from the building as a precaution - No gunshots fired during the event - The noises heard were presumably of pyrotechnic origin
## Key facts - **What**: Police intervention for reports of alleged gunshots - When: Night between 4 and 5 September - Where: High school center in Goldach, Canton of St. Gallen - Who: Canton of St. Gallen police - People involved: About 300 students and staff
The police intervention in Goldach concluded in the night, following a report received by the operations center during a school party. Authorities were alerted by several calls reporting alleged gunshots heard inside the high school center. As a precautionary measure, the police led the students and teaching staff inside the building, simultaneously initiating standard safety procedures for such alerts.
### Facts The Canton of St. Gallen police confirmed that, following investigations on the scene, there was no gunfire. The spokesperson for the institution clarified that the explosion noises heard by those present during the school party likely came from pyrotechnic objects used on that occasion. The operation, which saw the deployment of several patrols, special units, and support from police forces from neighboring cantons, officially ended around 2:00 AM. The evacuation of the approximately 300 people present in the area was completed by 1:00 AM, allowing all participants to return to their homes safely. No injuries were reported during the event or in the subsequent phases of the alert.
